results.title: US charges 14 over North Korean IT worker scheme at more than 70 companies
results.author: Ana-Maria Stanciuc
results.content:
The US Justice Department has charged 14 people over a North Korean job scam, announced on Tuesday. North Korean IT workers used stolen names to get remote jobs at more than 70 US firms.
The workers earned about $3 million, which went to North Korean groups under US sanctions, prosecutors believe. The firm works in health, telecoms, cyber support, retail, and manufacturing across 17 states and Washington, DC.
Moreover, two US nationals, from Pennsylvania and Texas, have been arrested. They and 12 others, including 10 people based in China, are charged with wire fraud, money laundering, and identity theft in Ohio.
Two of the defendants have not been named, and the charges are allegations; all defendants are presumed innocent.
From 2019 to around July 2025, the workers used fake or stolen ID papers to apply, the indictment says. Online tools made it look as if they were working from inside the US.
They also paid helpers in the US to run so-called laptop farms. The helpers kept work laptops at home and set them up so the workers could use them from abroad. They then moved the pay to accounts run by North Korea, prosecutors said.
In a separate operation in September, the FBI searched more than 40 homes in Texas suspected of being laptop farms. It seized about 187 laptops and other devices.
“North Korea’s rogue regime uses its pervasive IT worker schemes to raise revenue for various illicit purposes, including the development of weapons that could ultimately target the United States or its allies,” said John Eisenberg, the assistant attorney general for national security.
The FBI also issued a new warning to companies as North Korean workers are increasingly hiring Americans to help them avoid detection, and some pass whole jobs on to other foreign nationals, it said.
Security firm CrowdStrike, which helped the FBI, tracks the group as ‘Famous Chollima’. North Korean hackers have also built their own AI tools for attacks, and hidden malware in fake software packages aimed at coders.

results.summary:
The U.S. Department of Justice has charged 14 individuals for operating a sophisticated scheme where North Korean IT workers infiltrated over 70 American companies using stolen identities.

### Key Points
- Prosecutors allege the workers earned $3 million to fund North Korean state activities while working remotely in sectors like healthcare, telecommunications, and manufacturing.
- The indictment names 14 defendants, including two U.S. nationals from Pennsylvania and Texas and 10 individuals based in China, on charges of wire fraud and money laundering.
- Between 2019 and 2025, the group utilized "laptop farms" in the U.S. to mask their overseas locations and bypass corporate security protocols.
- The FBI recently seized 187 devices from over 40 locations in Texas suspected of facilitating these remote work operations.
- Security firm CrowdStrike identifies the group behind these activities as "Famous Chollima," noting their use of malware and AI tools to target software developers.

### Why it Matters
This scheme highlights significant vulnerabilities in remote hiring practices that allow foreign actors to infiltrate sensitive U.S. corporate networks. Companies must now implement more rigorous identity verification and device monitoring to prevent state-sponsored entities from siphoning revenue and accessing proprietary data.

results.title: The winners and losers of the new H-1B era
results.author: Charissa Cheong,Alex Nicoll,Madison Hoff,Aditi Bharade
results.content:
The new H-1B reality is beginning to produce clear winners and losers.
The Trump administration has introduced proposals that target various legal immigration pathways, from the H-1B visa for highly skilled foreign workers to the OPT student work authorization for foreign students who have graduated from a US university.
On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance announced a crackdown on the pathway to green cards for workers at some tech firms, including Microsoft and Adobe.
Business Insider has been covering how skilled foreign workers navigate the changing immigration policies through our ongoing H-1B fallout series, launched one year after Trump first introduced the $100,000 fee on some H-1B applicants. We have examined where foreign talent is heading and the hidden sacrifices of those who opt into the H-1B system. We've also spotlighted stories from individuals at different stages of the visa pipeline.
To understand who is better and worse off in the new H-1B system, Business Insider spoke to immigration lawyers and academics and analyzed H-1B application data from the first three quarters of the last three fiscal years.
Ted Chiappari, head of immigration law at law firm Duane Morris, told Business Insider there is nothing in any of the changes in H-1B rules or policies that "would favor one company over another."
Instead, what's emerging is that employers with cash and employees with in-demand skills are seeing a relative advantage from the increasingly uncertain H-1B regime.
The US issues 85,000 H-1B visas a year. Demand still outweighs supply, even as applications in the March 2026 H-1B lottery dropped more than 38% from the year before, the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services said.
Trump's proposed $100,000 H-1B fee for new applicants is held up in the courts. It is "probably the main reason" those applications fell, Chiappari said.
The administration has previously said its changes are intended to curb misuse of the H-1B program and protect American workers, a sentiment echoed by USCIS. Spokesperson Zach Kahler said the goal is to have employment-based visas "supplement, not supplant American workers."
The White House and the Department of Labor did not respond to requests for comment.
Winner: High salary, high specialization workers
A regulatory change that favors one group of workers over another is the wage-weighted H-1B cap selection. It replaced the randomized lottery earlier this year and gives applicants in higher wage bands a greater chance of being selected.
They get another boost by simple arithmetic. If you're going to potentially pay $100,000 more than someone's salary in order to hire them, you likely would only do it for someone who is making quite a bit above $100,000.
It's evident in some of the largest hiring increases in the data, which are directly tied to generative AI trends. Data scientists saw the number of certified H-1B applications go up by nearly a quarter year-over-year in 2026, the largest of any other job category with more than 5,000 applications. The smaller category of computer and information research scientists saw their applications go up nearly 40%. These are high-paying occupations: As of May 2025, data scientists earned a median annual salary of $120,230, and computer and information research scientists made $140,300, both well above the overall median annual wage of $50,980.
Certified applications are not the same as visas issued and may include updates to information on existing employees, but the data can provide insight into the state of the H-1B system. Data that shows the full scope of the fiscal year's H-1B hires is expected to be released later this year.
Catherine Macris, a partner at the immigration law firm Fragomen, said that employees in highly specialized, high-demand fields — like tech — might be better positioned because recent changes have placed increased emphasis on "specialization, compensation levels, and employer compliance readiness."
Specialized roles don't just command higher salaries; they also "align more readily with evolving H-1B eligibility and wage considerations," Macris said. It's easier to show that they're actual specialists who need to be hired internationally rather than domestically.
Winner: Tech employers
Tech employers rapidly building out generative AI have been one of the biggest pillars of the economy in the last couple of years. The story is no different with H-1B visas.
Tech companies are among the top employers that recruit highly skilled talent and maintain robust immigration policies and compliance programs, potentially making them better positioned to navigate the current environment, Fragomen's Macris said.
Among a select group of Big Tech employers, certified applications were only down about 6.5%, compared to 10% for all total applications. At rapidly growing AI giants like Nvidia, Anthropic, and OpenAI, applications are shooting up especially quickly, highlighting how closely tied hiring changes are to broader economic trends.
Loser: Small startups that can't afford the $100K fee
Smaller startups, without the money or legal departments to try their hands with the H-1B lottery, are another likely loser, said Gaurav Khanna, a UC San Diego associate economics professor.
"Big companies like Nvidia and Salesforce are not deterred by such fees, but smaller startups are," he said. This could have a stifling effect on innovation from the startup sector, he said.
Loser: Companies that transfer foreign workers from overseas
Companies with large international presences that transfer employees from overseas to the US are "most susceptible to the restrictive policies," said Lynden Melmed, a partner at the immigration law firm BAL.
Professional services companies that can already outsource work overseas will have an increasingly hard time making the case for bringing workers stateside.
Khanna said he would guess that the overall impact has been hardest on outsourcers like Infosys, TCS, and Cognizant, as well as those that rely on these outsourcers for tech talent. Those three employers saw their certified applications fall in aggregate by 30% year-over-year.
Vice President JD Vance's comments on October 8 underscored the administration's stance on the outsourcing firms that help third-party corporations bring overseas workers to the US.
"These firms are as complicit, or maybe more so complicit, in the visa fraud than any American corporation," Vance said.
Accounting firms, or at least their employees overseas, face a similar problem. Accountant and audit professional certified applications were down 25% year over year.
Certified filings for the Big Four accounting firms are also down around 30% year-over-year.
Loser: Universities, recent grads, and entry-level employees
Recent graduates and early-career professionals might naturally lose out due to their lower earning potential. Fragomen's Macris said employers who rely heavily on early-career talent, such as accounting and consulting firms with large campus recruiting programs, "may also experience greater pressure" because of this framework.
Their challenges stand in contrast to the relative success of highly paid, highly trained employees.
As for the institutions training these workers, they're also facing an uphill battle, said Chiappari, as they don't have the same deep pockets as other employers to stomach the costs and uncertainty of the current H-1B regime.
The top 50 schools on the 2027 U.S. News & World Report ranking saw their certified applications fall by 14% from 2025 to 2026.
results.summary:
The Trump administration’s restrictive H-1B visa policies and proposed $100,000 fees are reshaping the labor market, favoring high-salary tech specialists while creating significant hurdles for startups and outsourcing firms.

### Key Points
- The March 2026 H-1B lottery saw a 38% decline in applications, largely attributed to a proposed $100,000 fee currently facing legal challenges.
- A new wage-weighted selection process prioritizes higher-paid applicants, benefiting roles in generative AI like data scientists and research scientists.
- Major tech companies, including Nvidia, Anthropic, and OpenAI, remain resilient, while outsourcing firms like Infosys, TCS, and Cognizant saw certified applications drop by 30%.
- Small startups and accounting firms are struggling to navigate the increased costs and compliance requirements of the current immigration regime.
- Certified H-1B applications for graduates from top-ranked universities fell by 14% between 2025 and 2026.

### Why it Matters
These policy shifts are fundamentally altering the U.S. talent pipeline by favoring established, capital-rich corporations over smaller innovators and entry-level professionals. This environment may stifle startup growth and reduce the availability of early-career opportunities, potentially impacting long-term economic competitiveness in the technology sector.

results.title: Battle lines shift in House races as Republicans retreat from front-line districts
results.author: THOMAS BEAUMONT Associated Press, JOEY CAPPELLETTI Associated Press, MIKE CATALINI Associated Press
results.content:
Battle lines shift in House races as Republicans retreat from front-line districts
Republicans are retreating from several key U.S. House races, while Democrats are racing to raise funds for candidates who seemed unlikely to win earlier this year
DES MOINES, Iowa -- Republicans were retreating Tuesday from a handful of battleground U.S. House races while Democrats were racing to raise money to boost candidates who seemed like long shots earlier this year.
The Congressional Leadership Fund, the leading House Republican super PAC, canceled spending in four races from the Midwest to the East Coast and increased its investment in 16 other races from Texas to Pennsylvania. Another super PAC allied with President Donald Trump is cutting back in a battleground district in the Las Vegas area.
The decisions were disclosed by three Republican campaign officials familiar with the plans who spoke on condition of anonymity to share private strategy conversations.
Meanwhile, Democrats' House campaign committee is eyeing openings in Republican-held districts and hoping to raise millions of dollars in the next week to fuel a late round of advertising that they say could net at least a half dozen more seats.
The shifting money in the final three weeks of midterm campaigns points to an increasingly defensive posture by Republicans, who have already trimmed their expectations in U.S. Senate races, and new aggression from Democrats, who are trying to capitalize on President Donald Trump's weak approval ratings.
“You can tell now where people are competing based on where they’re putting the money,” said Stu Sandler, a Republican strategist working on House and statewide races this year.
David McIntosh, president of the conservative Club For Growth, said there are only a few places where Republicans could pick up seats this year.
"The economic environment has not been good," he said. “Voters are dissatisfied with their Republican majority and the base is also dissatisfied with that they weren’t able to get the SAVE America Act passed,” referring to Trump's plan for a strict proof-of-citizenship voting bill.
“It looked like Republicans were weak,” McIntosh said, “and so you’ve seen a lot of drop-off in enthusiasm.”
The Congressional Leadership Fund is no longer spending on advertising in Iowa's 1st District, where three-term Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks is defending her seat against Democrat Christina Bohannan.
Bohannan is running for her third time against Miller-Meeks. Last time, the race was decided by only 799 votes, making it the second-closest in the country. It's an eastern Iowa district where congressional cuts to Medicaid have been linked to hospital service closures and high diesel prices have been a challenge for farmers.
Likewise, the officials said the group won't keep spending in New Jersey's 7th District, where second-term Republican Rep. Tom Kean is facing off against Democrat Rebecca Bennett. Kean has been under scrutiny for his four-month absence from Congress, which he left unexplained until disclosing a mental health crisis upon his return. Kean, who won by 5.4 percentage points two years ago, has also faced questions over his support for Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war.
These races, as well as one in the Cincinnati, Ohio, area and one in east-central Michigan, have accounted for $13.3 million in Congressional Leadership Fund spending, more than 12% of its total through Oct. 13.
The group will instead reinforce districts where Trump beat Democrat Kamala Harris by narrow margins in 2024.
Safety and Affordability, an offshoot of MAGA Inc., pulled nearly $1 million in ad spending aimed at helping Republican Marty O’Donnell’s campaign in Nevada’s 3rd District. Republicans had hoped that Trump's tax-cut legislation — specifically no taxes on tips — would resonate in Las Vegas and help defeat Democratic Rep. Susie Lee, who voted against the bill.
Sandler said his party needs to turn out voters who usually participate in presidential elections but often stay home in the midterms.
“One thing you can’t say is that they’ve been under-resourced,” he said. “Republican resources are at a high. They’ve never been this well-funded in the midterm.”
As House Republicans have retrenched, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee believes at least a dozen more races could be within striking distance. However, they need more money to take advantage.
The committee launched a $17 million fundraising drive, with a deadline of Oct. 22, to pump advertising onto the air in districts that were once seen as out of reach.
“It’s not that we need the money to win in the districts where we have been running to get to 218 seats,” said Courtney Rice, the committee’s communication director. “We’re talking about the next level.”
One is Ohio's 10th, a Dayton-area district represented by 12-term Republican Rep. Mike Turner. Democrats see Turner as beatable despite the former Dayton mayor's durability and 18 percentage-point victory two years ago. Trump carried the district by six percentage points in 2024.
Turner didn't begin advertising until late September, according to AdImpact, later than most competitive House incumbents, and the National Republican Congressional Committee started spending there this week.
If the Democratic committee reaches its goal, it would also start spending in the Miami area, suburban St. Louis, Missouri and the Little Rock, Arkansas, area. They would be able to buy ads in coordination with the campaigns at the lower rate available to candidates, due to a June Supreme Court decision, squeezing more ad time from those dollars.
Senate Republicans are pouring millions more into Nebraska to protect Sen. Pete Ricketts, the latest sign of how dramatically their spending priorities have shifted from battleground states toward defending seats they once expected to hold comfortably.
Ricketts is facing a challenge from independent Dan Osborn, who is backed by Democrats. Trump won Nebraska by more than 20 percentage points in 2024.
The Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, said Tuesday it was behind a $15 million investment in the state.
Other groups are also pumping money into the race, with the cryptocurrency-backed super PAC Fairshake launching a $7 million advertising campaign, according to AdImpact data.
The group has also increased its investment in Ohio’s Senate race, bringing its total spending there to $45 million in support of Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who is up against Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown.
The Nebraska investment follows new spending by the Senate Leadership Fund in Kansas and South Carolina, two other states Trump won by double digits in 2024. All three were absent from the group’s initial $342 million advertising plan in April, which has since been reshaped as Republicans pulled back from Georgia and North Carolina, two states that were central to their original strategy.
Democrats are also shifting their resources. The Senate Democrats’ main spending arm said Tuesday it was pulling its advertising last week from Georgia, where Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has built a substantial fundraising advantage over Republican Rep. Mike Collins, and focusing instead on Maine, New Hampshire, Michigan, Iowa, Kansas, Texas, Alaska and Ohio.
The shifting investments come as both parties make their final spending decisions in the battle for Senate control, with Democrats pointing to their candidates and the political environment as potential counterweights to Republican money.
In a letter to fellow senators Tuesday, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said the battle for control of the chamber “comes down to one defining question.”
“Will the unprecedented tsunami of Republican money defeat the massive Democratic advantage in candidates, policies, and political climate?” Schumer asked.
results.summary:
Republican super PACs are shifting campaign funds away from several competitive House districts to defend vulnerable seats, while Democrats launch aggressive fundraising drives to capitalize on new opportunities.

### Key Points
- The Congressional Leadership Fund canceled spending in four House races across Iowa, New Jersey, Ohio, and Michigan to prioritize 16 other competitive districts.
- A pro-Trump super PAC withdrew nearly $1 million in advertising support for Republican candidate Marty O’Donnell in Nevada’s 3rd District.
- The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee initiated a $17 million fundraising drive to expand advertising into previously unreachable districts, including Ohio’s 10th.
- Senate Republicans committed $15 million to protect Senator Pete Ricketts in Nebraska, reflecting a broader trend of defending seats in traditionally safe states.
- Cryptocurrency-backed super PAC Fairshake increased its total spending to $45 million to support Republican Senator Jon Husted in Ohio.

### Why it Matters
These strategic reallocations signal a defensive posture for Republicans as they struggle to maintain their majority amid shifting voter enthusiasm and economic concerns. The movement of millions of dollars in the final weeks of the campaign highlights how both parties are rapidly adjusting their maps to secure control of Congress.

results.title: The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is almost the Android tablet we needed
results.author: David Pierce
results.content:
We have to talk about this screen. It’s the first thing you notice, and maybe the only thing that matters, about the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. It’s a 12-inch, 2800 x 1840 panel with a new technology Amazon calls “Nanomatte” that is meant to decrease glare and increase the feeling that you can reach out and touch the things you see onscreen. When Amazon set out to build the best tablet the company has ever shipped, it started with this screen.
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is almost the Android tablet we needed
The screen is gorgeous, the hardware works, and it finally runs full Android. But there’s too much Amazon in my tablet.
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is almost the Android tablet we needed
The screen is gorgeous, the hardware works, and it finally runs full Android. But there’s too much Amazon in my tablet.
The $549.99 device I’ve been testing is one of four new models in the Alexa Tablet lineup, which ranges from a $229.99 8-inch model up to a $679.99 12 Pro with this Nanomatte coating and some extra RAM you don’t really need. The pitch for all those devices is the same: They’re well-made, midrange tablets that can access the full universe of Android apps through the Play Store and come with a whole bunch of Amazon bloatware whether you want it or not. I haven’t tested those other devices, but I’m glad they exist — cheap, good Android tablets are too hard to come by.
The Good
- Screen is gorgeous
- Android apps!
- Nice design and build quality
The Bad
- Amazon bloatware everywhere
- Alexa Plus isn’t great
- Some middling specs
But the Nanomatte. The Nanomatte! The etching on the display, which Amazon says it partnered with Corning to do at a sub-pixel level to reduce glare without causing the slight rainbow-shimmering effect you can get on other matte screens, absolutely does its job. When I use my iPad outdoors, I can often see what’s behind me like I’m staring into a mirror; the 12 Pro reflects only a small sheen of light, and does it without losing any sharpness. The viewing angles are incredible, too. I’d like the display to be a little brighter, but since the main reason to crank the brightness is to fight glare, it hasn’t really been a problem.
The screen is not perfect. The anti-glare texture gives the Alexa Tablet a bit of shimmer, especially when you’re looking at light text on a black background. And the iPad’s blacks are still blacker; watching a movie, the letterboxes above and below are still slightly lit on the Alexa Tablet’s LCD, and they’re just flat-out off on the iPad’s OLED panel. Some of this you can fix: The 12 Pro has specific modes that automatically tweak tone and color to make reading more pleasant, and you can even control the overall picture through a few presets like the ones you’d find on your TV. My review unit came with “Boosted” mode turned on, which made every color just a smidge too colorful. I turned it to “Natural” and immediately liked the picture better.
I’m not sure this screen counts as some revolution in display technology, but then again, I did reflexively say “whoa” the first second I turned it on, and all that was showing was the Amazon logo. I like this display for everything. The 120Hz refresh rate looks great when running Star Wars: Galactic Racer, and the 3:2 aspect ratio feels right for web browsing and side-by-side work. The more muted display modes even make reading more pleasant than your average giant screen, though it’s lame that they only work in the Kindle app. After a few days of using the tablet indoors and out, I prefer the 12 Pro’s screen to any iPad I’ve tried. (Unfortunately, I don’t have an iPad Pro with the nano-texture glass to compare it to, but that’s a $2,200 tablet. I doubt anyone’s debating between the two.)
All that display tech in a $549.99 device requires tradeoffs basically everywhere else, and Amazon makes lots of them. The MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor benchmarks somewhere between a flagship high-end Android phone from last year and a flagship phone from two years ago, and gets absolutely lapped by practically every current iPad. In one graphics-heavy benchmark, the current 13-inch iPad Pro scored about nine times higher.
I’d like more horsepower here, but in my day-to-day use there’s plenty of power in this tablet. In several days of playing games, doing work, and watching a lot of NFL RedZone, the only slowness I’ve detected has been little niggling things in the Android experience. The app switcher sometimes stutters when it loads. I suppose I worry a little about how this tablet will age, given that it doesn’t share the iPad’s preposterous oversupply of processing power, but for now it’s fine.
Come to think of it, “it’s fine” explains most of the 12 Pro’s hardware. The four speakers are a little thin and muddy, but loud and clear enough. The cameras wash out some colors, but they work for video calls. The $149.99 keyboard case is nice to type on, but a little awkward to detach and manipulate. The $89.99 pen is smooth and responsive, but not many Android apps support a stylus. The battery lasts me about eight hours of screen time, which is a little less than I’d like and less than Amazon advertises. Nothing here is a deal-breaker, it’s just a lot of fine.
The software, on the other hand, is all extremes. The great news: The Alexa Tablets run full Android, not the weird off-brand operating system Amazon’s Fire tablets have used for the last 15 years. That means you get all the apps in the Play Store, a vastly improved interface, and access to things like Google’s Gemini assistant. All by itself, that change makes these the most functional Amazon tablets ever.
Unfortunately, Amazon did to Android exactly what you’d fear — and maybe expect. It Amazon-ed the crap out of things. I’m fine with the slide-over panel to the left of the homescreen filled with content recommendations; the overlap of Alexa Tablet owners and Prime subscribers / Kindle readers is probably pretty high, and at least that screen isn’t staring you in the face every time you unlock your tablet. I can even live with Amazon preloading its own browser, photos, and music apps, none of which are better than their competition. But it is frankly outrageous that Amazon thinks it can get away with adding two separate, non-removable homescreen widgets that serve no purpose other than advertising Amazon’s products.
If you’re going to say you “obsess over customers,” you don’t get to borrow the top left corner of my homescreen and then use that space to show me an ad vaguely offering to “Cook with premium ingredients” that launches an also unhideable Alexa chat window in the bottom right corner of my homescreen.
Luckily, this is Android, and installing a new launcher takes 30 seconds. If you buy an Alexa Tablet, I recommend doing so immediately.
I would be less annoyed by Alexa’s overbearing presence on this tablet if Alexa Plus were actually useful, which it mostly is not. If you’re looking to buy whatever’s on your screen, Alexa’s your bot: You can invoke the assistant in any app, and it’ll almost always assume your goal is to shop for whatever you’re currently looking at. If you want, well, anything else, you’re probably out of luck. Almost a year after its launch, Alexa Plus is not a very good assistant. It’s slow, it gets lost in back-and-forth conversations, and it still doesn’t have enough access to my apps and data to be useful. You can switch to Gemini in the device’s settings, and you should.
Once you de-Amazon the tablet, you’re left with a pretty useful Android device. And this is where the Alexa Tablet gets tricky to evaluate. I wouldn’t recommend using it as a primary computer, given the still sorry state of large-screen Android apps. (Between this and the ongoing Googlebook fiasco, I really hope Google is learning a lesson about incentivizing developers to care about big screens and keyboards.) But between the Kindle-specific display mode, all the streaming and reading apps in the Play Store, and this terrific screen, this is immediately one of the best tablets-for-tablet-things you can buy.
Realistically, you’re probably debating whether to buy the Alexa Tablet or an iPad. (Apologies to the Samsung Galaxy Tab shoppers out there, but this one’s a way better buy for almost everybody.) For the same $550 you’ll drop on the 12 Pro, you can get a base-model iPad with 256GB of storage. I’d probably tell you to buy the iPad; it has much better tablet software and much better big-screen apps, and Apple has a much better track record in tablets.
And yet for the last few days, I’ve had an iPad and an Alexa Tablet sitting on my desk, and every time I want to watch or read something I’ve found myself gravitating to Amazon’s device. It is really nice to look at.
results.summary:
The new Alexa Tablet 12 Pro features a high-quality 12-inch Nanomatte display and full Android support, offering a compelling alternative to the iPad despite heavy pre-installed Amazon software.

### Key Points
- The 12-inch display uses Corning-partnered Nanomatte technology to significantly reduce glare while maintaining sharpness.
- Pricing for the new lineup starts at $229.99 for the 8-inch model, with the 12 Pro model retailing for $549.99.
- The device runs full Android with Google Play Store access, marking a departure from Amazon’s traditional Fire OS.
- Hardware includes a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor, a 120Hz refresh rate, and a 3:2 aspect ratio screen.
- The tablet comes pre-loaded with non-removable Amazon advertising widgets and the Alexa Plus assistant, which users can replace with Google Gemini.

### Why it Matters
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro represents a significant shift for Amazon by adopting a standard Android interface, making it a more versatile competitor in the premium tablet market. While the hardware and display quality offer a strong value proposition, the aggressive integration of Amazon’s ecosystem and advertising may require users to customize the software to achieve a clean experience.

results.title: 'What companies are facing today is an AI zoo' — NordLayer warns that dozens of unsanctioned chatbots are quietly widening every company's exposure to data leaks
results.author: Efosa Udinmwen
results.content:
- AI Scout tracks which artificial intelligence services employees actually use at work
- Employees are increasingly turning to AI services outside approved channels
- NordLayer AI Scout can warn, redact, or block sensitive prompts before submission
Employees are increasingly using AI tools at work, including services their employers may not have approved or formally provided.
That creates uncertainty about which AI platforms workers access, what information they submit, and how those systems connect with business operations.
NordLayer says its new AI Scout tool will now help give organizations visibility into workplace AI activity and the security risks associated with it.
Seeing actual AI use inside companies
The standalone product monitors browser and desktop interactions while providing controls intended to limit exposure of confidential information across systems.
AI Scout can identify authorized and unauthorized AI services, allowing organizations to compare observed activity against software approved for workplace use.
Its reporting measures usage from real activity rather than purchased subscriptions, and it also estimates token consumption across deployed LLMs.
It also examines information employees send to AI systems, using controls designed to detect potentially sensitive material before certain prompts are submitted.

The company says these safeguards operate before submission, potentially preventing confidential material from reaching an external AI service.
NordLayer also says browser-based controls can intervene when employees enter information requiring additional scrutiny before transmission.
The monitoring extends beyond conventional chatbot use into AI agents and their technical relationships with connected services used at work.
Administrators can inspect MCP infrastructure linked to programming agents and review the capabilities available through those systems in practice.
“We built NordLayer AI Scout for how AI actually works — not just what it looks like from the outside, but for what’s happening at a technical level,” says Vakaris Noreika, VP of product research and development at NordLayer.
“Its AI DLP is designed to inspect prompts and control them pre-submission, to ensure that sensitive data is never inputted in the first place.
Why workplace AI needs closer oversight
The need for monitoring comes as business investment in artificial intelligence grows alongside employee use of unapproved services, a practice known as shadow AI.
Writer's 2026 enterprise survey found that 59% of companies spend more than $1 million annually on artificial intelligence technology.
A University of Melbourne report cited by NordLayer found that 42% of employees use approved AI systems, while 70% use free models at work.
IBM reports that breaches involving shadow AI add $400,000 to the global average breach cost of $4.99 million worldwide.
Those figures help explain why organizations may struggle to maintain visibility when employees use AI services beyond formally approved platforms.
“What companies are facing today is an AI zoo — dozens of unsanctioned LLMs in daily use across the workforce, each one widening the organization’s exposure to data leaks and security breaches,” says Andrius Buinovskis, VP of product strategy at NordLayer.
“True AI governance requires extensive visibility. With new LLM solutions emerging at a rapid pace, reviewing every new AI tool manually simply doesn’t scale — organizations need telemetry that brings all AI use, sanctioned or not, into one platform.”

results.title: Linux doesn’t need antivirus the way Windows does, but not for the reason most people think
results.author: Anmol Mehrotra
results.content:
Linux has forever been considered above Windows when it comes to security. Part of the reason for that, and what people usually assume, is that Linux doesn't have a meaningful market share for attackers to target with sophisticated malware or attacks. While that holds true when compared to Windows's market share, it definitely is not the full picture. Linux also has an advanced permission management system that usually prevents files from being accessed or executed, which provides additional security. I tested this by setting up WSL and an Ubuntu installation, then letting it scan my data, including a file infected with make-believe malware, to see how it responded.
Attackers do target Linux
The AUR campaign went after trust, not market share
Let's look at what happened earlier this year when hackers decided that Linux had enough users to launch an attack. In June 2026, Arch User Repository (AUR) was compromised by hackers who injected malware into over 400 packages. The attackers adopted abandoned packages and edited their build instructions, so installing them also pulled in an npm package called atomic-lockfile to deliver rootkit-like malware. Sonatype later noted that an estimated roughly 1,500 packages across AUR were impacted and were modified to steal credentials. Since then, AI has credentials.
Linux’s defaults make attackers work harder
A downloaded script does nothing until you allow it
Linux permission setup does not allow files to be executable by default without explicit user permission. This ensures that malware that was downloaded or transferred to a Linux system is not executed automatically. I tested this by asking my Ubuntu CLI to run a simple one-line script, which it denied because the system didn't have enough permissions to run it. System folders work in a similar way, and running a command to create a new file simply failed.
One caveat, of course, was that my account on Ubuntu is set up in the sudo group, so the system safety was more or less fully in my hands. Good terminal habits can be a life-saver when it comes to Linux, especially if you are logged in as admin or using sudo. One of the reasons for the AUR attack was that users probably ran packages without reviewing changes, allowing malicious code to run on the system.
Antivirus flags only what it recognizes
ClamAV is good at known files, not at trust decisions
I installed ClamAV on my copy of Ubuntu and downloaded its database of about 3.6 million entries. Once done, I created an EICAR test file on my system. For those unaware, an EICAR test file is a harmless 68-byte to 128-byte dummy malware file created by the European Institute for Computer Antivirus Research (EICAR) and the Computer Antivirus Research Organization to test antivirus. ClamAV was quick to flag the file as infected when I ran the virus scan and reported EICAR-signature FOUND straight away.
However, this is half the story. Antivirus like ClamAV is great at recognizing known threats and malware but falls short with new malware, or malware that isn't obvious or is embedded in the executable. That's where things differ for Linux: having antivirus, while good practice, doesn't make you fully secure against threats.
Running a scanner anyway is reasonable
It helps ensure your system does not have files that can cause harm
As mentioned above, antivirus is only half the story on Linux, and Linux permissions limit the damage if you accidentally download malware. This is why people often don't need antivirus on Linux as long as they follow good habits, like not giving every file or folder full permissions and ensuring packages come from trusted sources.
Another tip that works wonders is to always check what changed when a package was recently updated. Also, ensure the package is coming from a trusted source and is not modified by a middleman.
The obvious counterpoint email attachments.
Linux’s real protection is a habit, not a product
Keep ClamAV for scanning files and keep your trust decisions for yourself
Linux is generally safer than Windows because of its permission system, how it handles packages, and its rapid patching of bugs and vulnerabilities, plus a smaller user base than Windows or macOS, which makes it less lucrative for attackers looking to do maximum damage.
Overall, this makes a case for Linux not needing an antivirus in the traditional sense, like one would for Windows or a Mac. However, tools like ClamAV can provide an extra layer of security against known threats.
The threat landscape is changing, and it is changing rapidly thanks to AI tools that can comb through data and lines of code to find vulnerabilities that can be targeted. So the notion that Linux doesn't require any security is outdated and, frankly, dangerous. However, the good news is that if you follow good security hygiene, keep your system updated, and exercise caution when downloading or running unverified scripts, you should be in a good place.
results.summary:
While Linux is often considered more secure than Windows due to its robust permission architecture, recent incidents demonstrate that users must remain vigilant against evolving cybersecurity threats.

### Key Points
- In June 2026, hackers compromised the Arch User Repository (AUR), injecting rootkit-like malware into approximately 1,500 packages to steal user credentials.
- Linux security relies heavily on a permission system that prevents files from executing automatically without explicit user authorization.
- Antivirus software like ClamAV effectively detects known threats but often fails to identify new, sophisticated, or embedded malware.
- Security experts recommend maintaining good digital hygiene, such as verifying package sources and reviewing code changes, rather than relying solely on antivirus tools.

### Why it Matters
The misconception that Linux is immune to malware is increasingly dangerous as attackers leverage AI to identify and exploit vulnerabilities. Adopting proactive security habits is essential for users to protect their systems against modern, targeted campaigns that bypass traditional defenses.
