results.title: Who Is Planting Backdoors in Ledger Crypto Wallets?
results.author: Kim Zetter
results.content:
After crypto wallet maker Ledger announced Friday that a backdoor embedded in a handful of Ledger wallets sold in SouthEast Asia allowed thieves to hijack around $102 million in crypto from their owners, news has emerged of other Ledger wallets sold in Germany also having implants.
The hardware implants were originally found on an unknown number of Ledger Nano X wallets sold by an authorized Ledger reseller called CryptoBilis based in Malaysia. Ledger said the implants were found on a limited number of devices, all sold by the same seller. But a Ledger device owner in Europe has since said that he found an implant on a Nano X that he purchased at a large European electronics chain store in August and a second one he purchased this weekend at another store in the same chain. He believes these indicate that Ledger’s supply-chain has been compromised.
Since then, users and researchers have also reported finding implants in Ledger Flex and Ledger Stax devices – two of Ledger's more recent line of devices used for securely storing keys used to access a device owner's crypto accounts.
The implants are not the first to be found on Ledger wallets. Famed hardware hacker Joe Grand found implants on several Nano X wallets earlier this year and notified Ledger about them in March, raising questions about Ledger's urgency in addressing the issue. Many of the implants discovered more recently appear to be more sophisticated iterations of the ones that Grand found.
The implants Grand discovered were also all in wallets sold by unauthorized online sellers who seemingly ran fly-by-night operations that weren’t in business for long. But the implants found in wallets sold by CryptoBilis and the European electronics chain indicate the attackers have switched tactics and may be deliberately compromising wallets sold by authorized resellers now. Ledger and its competitor Trezor have cautioned users for years to buy wallets only from their web sites or from authorized resellers. But the recent compromises indicate that attackers are deliberately targeting authorized sellers to exploit customer trust in them and to get wider distribution for implanted devices. What’s more, the attackers have become more skilled and systematic in their method for compromising the wallets, making it more difficult to detect the implants, Grand and other researchers say.
It's not clear how long the implants have been sitting in the sold devices, but last week a coordinated heist resulted in millions of dollars in crypto being stolen from the device and accountholders. According to blockchain research company Bitquery, crypto was stolen from about 315 accounts connected to compromised CryptoBilis Ledger devices alone, and is currently valued at around $102 million. The stolen funds include Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tron and other cryptocurrencies. Some of the funds have reportedly been frozen in the accounts to which the thieves transferred it, and other funds appear to be in accounts that have been flagged for fraud. And it's not clear if funds were also stolen from Ledger owners who purchased their devices from other sellers.
Ledger, based in France, wrote in statement posted to X that it had asked CryptoBilis to halt all sales and shipments of Ledger devices until it could conduct an investigation. CryptoBilis — which is authorized to sell Ledger wallets in Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines — wrote on its web site that it is cooperating with Ledger’s investigation.
But a user going by the name Johannes wrote on X over the weekend that he had purchased a Ledger Nano X wallet in person from a MediaMarkt store that had an implant. MediaMarkt is Germany’s equivalent to BestBuy and has 1,000 stores in ten European countries. It’s listed as an authorized reseller of Ledger wallets in Austria, Germany, Spain and Turkey.
Johannes told Zero Day he purchased the wallet in August in a MediaMarkt store in Germany but only took the device apart this weekend following reports that implants had been found. He posted photos of an antenna and implant in his device. Johannes said that he has had no crypto stolen.
In an update to X this weekend, Ledger suggested the implant problem may stem from authorized resellers obtaining Ledger wallets from illegitimate sources or reselling wallets that were bought and returned to them — after being compromised.
“We are reminding our authorized resellers and distributors to source products only through authorized channels and never to restock returned products,” Ledger wrote. “This is an ongoing threat that doesn’t just impact Ledger, but the whole ecosystem, and we are calling others in the space to work with us on making improvements for users…. Raising the bar on physical supply-chain integrity benefits the entire ecosystem.”
But Johannes, who purchased a second Ledger wallet from another MediaMarkt store on Monday and found an implant in it as well thinks this suggests that Ledger’s supply chain has been compromised.
“This indicates a widespread issue rather than an isolated incident, potentially affecting Ledger inventory across MediaMarkt and Saturn stores throughout Europe,” he wrote on X. He says he initially thought his two compromised devices might have been return items that the store then resold as new, but a MediaMarkt employee told him they were new devices and that returns are sent back to Ledger, not re-sold.
Ledger did not respond to an inquiry from Zero Day, but the company wrote on X that there is currently "no indication that Ledger's security infrastructure, systems or services have been compromised.
The issue raises questions about Ledger’s response to the implants and its transparency to customers. After Grand notified the company last March about implants he found in Ledger wallets, the company told him it would investigate to determine who was behind the implants. But Grand says he never received any followup until months later when he asked about it, and someone at Ledger told him they had found no evidence that someone had used the implants to steal crypto from device owners.
But the situation began to change after this.
In April and May, Grand published his implant findings online and gave two presentations about them at conferences in April and May. Mark Karpelès, a French businessman and former CEO of the infamous bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox who was charged with fraud following the collapse of his business, saw Grand's research online and decided to purchase Ledger wallets to see if he could find implants in them as well. He obtained two wallets and found more advanced iterations of the implant Grand discovered and published his findings online last month.
Karpelès's notoriety in the crypto world caused information about the implants to spread widely in the crypto community, which may be why the heists occurred last week. The attackers may have been waiting until they had amassed many wallets with large balances associated with them before pulling off a widespread heist of funds. But once news about the implants began to spread, this may have spurred the thieves to quickly grab as much crypto as they could from wallets already compromised, before wallet owners could move to protect those funds. Some people online have been praising Karpelès for exposing the implants and an operation that might have gone unnoticed for years until he wrote about it.
Evolving Backdoors
Grand began looking at Ledger wallets in August 2025 after someone published a Reddit post indicating he had found something in his Ledger Nano X wallet. The owner, who purchased the wallet from an online marketplace in Thailand, cracked opened the wallet’s casing and found extra circuitry that should not have been there. He sent the wallet to Grand to see if he could confirm it was a backdoor and determine what it was designed to do.
Inside the device, Grand found an extra board as well as an antenna, LTE module and eSIM. He determined that the implant was stealing the recovery seeds of infected wallets and transmitting them to the attackers. The implant would sit silently on the device until the owner initialized it and caused it to generate a random seed phrase – essentially a password stored on the Ledger device to allow the device holder to access their crypto account. As the device sent each character of the seed phrase to the device's small screen to display to the owner, the implant copied them and stored the data before subsequently using the LTE module, antenna and eSIM to connect to a nearby cell tower and transmit the seed to the hackers.
Grand, who runs Grand Idea Studio, was thrilled with the finding because although there have long been rumors and theoretical claims about hardware implants on wallets he had never seen one in the wild. He purchased eight more Ledger wallets from several online sellers in Thailand and found that four of them were compromised with similar implants. All of the ones Grand purchased came from "sketchy" sellers on Lazada, an e-commerce platform in SouthEast Asia that is a subsidiary of the Chinese company Alibaba Group. The devices were shipped from Thailand.
On March 4, Grand reported his findings to Ledger and had a Zoom call with a team there, and subsequently gave two talks about the backdoors at the Tropicon conference in April and at the Hardwear.IO conference in May and posted his slides online. He also continued to have some e-mail conversations with Ledger before moving to a Signal group chat with some technical staff there as well as with a researcher based in Japan who had purchased some wallets through online sellers there in March and found implants in them.
In September, Karpelès saw Grand’s research and obtained two Ledger wallets, including one purchased at half price from a Chinese seller on Amazon that arrived in a “flawless” shrink-wrapped box from Malaysia. He found implants inside both wallets and published his findings last month on the web site for Tibane Labs, which Karpelès owns and uses to conduct blockchain research and produce open-source tools. The implants operated similar to the ones Grand had found, but they were much more sophisticated in their design and more cleverly hidden to make them harder to spot inside a device.
Karpelès said the version Grand found appeared to be a prototype that had evolved over time. That first-generation involved a bundle of hand-soldered wires that stood out to anyone who opened the devices. The wires connected the implant to the Nano’s screen to grab each character of the randomly-generated seed as they were displayed on the screen.
The more advanced implant used an orange-colored, transparent, custom-built flexible circuit laid over the wallet’s original board and laminated flat onto it and soldered in select places, eliminating the need to solder wires that could be easily seen. To make room for the additional circuit, the hackers had replaced the original battery with a smaller one. Based on some markings, the implant appeared to have been assembled in December 2025 or later.
The second implant, which he found in the device shipped from Malaysia, was the most advanced. Inside the wallet, there appeared to be nothing to distinguish it from an unmodified Nano X device. But a thin black antenna running along the top edge of the board was a giveaway. But every other giveaway from the previous design had been eliminated. The orange flex circuit had been coated with the same black color as the legitimate Ledger board, allowing it to blend in with that component. Part numbers were scraped off, and the original battery was still there. The attackers had simply removed some padding that normally sat behind the screen to make room for the implant. Notably, the attackers had silk-screened a parts number — AC-A2016-NANO-V1.1 — onto the antenna, suggesting it was a custom-built component that had been manufactured to hijack Nano wallets at scale.
“‘NANO' names the target,” Karpelès wrote, “and ‘V1.1’ says it has already been through at least one revision. Someone designed and ordered RF parts for this one device. That is a production run, not a one-off.”
This third-generation version of the implant was “not a hobbyist’s build,” he wrote. “A flex PCB keyed to the Ledger’s own parts, a custom antenna already at its second revision, colour-matched coating and scraped markings all point to planning, a real budget, and a goal of mass production.”
On October 8, the day before the crypto heists went public, Karpelès began posting a series of messages on X about his findings and responding to questions about the implants he found. This is when news of the implants began to spread. The next day, news of the crypto heists emerged, raising questions about whether the attention Karpelès brought to the implants caused the attackers to launch their crypto heister sooner than they had originally planned.
Who Is Behind the Compromised Wallets?
Over the weekend, questions have arisen online about the founders of CryptoBilis and the fact that the company quietly switched owners in March — an acquisition that was not publicly disclosed until this weekend when users on X began pointing fingers at the founders and suggesting they might be behind the compromised devices or at least cooperating with the crypto thieves who stole money from the owners of compromised Ledger devices.
CryptoBilis co-founder Arravind Prabu rejected the accusations and revealed that his company had been acquired by someone else earlier this year and that he and his cofounder had “fully stepped down from all operations, system access, and management” in March. When asked why the acquisition was never made public, Prabu claimed in a lengthy statement that the deal was under an NDA until mid-October, which only enhanced suspicions.
“Since the completion of the handover, we have held zero access, credentials, visibility, or administrative control over CryptoBilis backend systems, customer databases, order histories, or corporate communication channels,” Prabu and his cofounder wrote in their statement. “Under the formal acquisition agreements, all parties were contractually bound to hold off on issuing a joint public announcement until mid-October 2026.”
He says that all suppliers — presumably Ledger among them — were “previously notified of the corporate acquisition and new management structure.”
Several people Zero Day spoke with say the months-long silence around the acquisition is "very shady" and question whether this was intended to keep Ledger customers in the dark while the implants spread through online sales. But Prabu says the suspicion, at least against them, is misplaced.
Oddly, Prabu did not identify who acquired CryptoBilis. He wrote that anyone who has questions about Ledger devices sold by CryptoBilis should contact Nicholas Chang. Chang, however, is identified in old postings to Facebook and X as a director of marketing for CryptoBilis, not the owner. Chang did not respond to an inquiry from Zero Day.
There is currently no evidence that anyone associated with CryptoBilis is behind the implants or the heist of cryptocurrency last week.
But the security researcher in Japan who has participated in conversations about the implants with Grand and Ledger since the spring, told Zero Day that he uncovered some intriguing findings from data he extracted from Ledger implants he purchased.
The researcher, who doesn't want to be publicly identified, purchased several Nano X wallets last March for his own use and put them in a drawer, intending to analyze them at some point when he had free time. After seeing Grand post his Tropicon slides online last spring, he took apart his own Ledger devices and found implants in them. He ended up purchasing ten Nano X devices from unauthorized Ledger sellers, most of them through the Amazon marketplace in Japan. One of the devices shipped from Malaysia, several came from Thailand, and two of them were shipped to him from an address in Osaka – essentially a shipping hub. All of them had implants. He found five different versions of implants among them, including the sophisticated implants Karpelès had found, as well as two additional designs.
"Some were very advanced and some were very basic," he says. "When I say versions [I mean] some of the layouts or components are different."
All of the implants operate in similar ways to record the randomly generated seed phrase as it's sent to the compromised device's screen and transmit the data to the attackers. He says he can't tell if the same group is behind all of the designs or if different actors took inspiration from an original design created by one person and advanced it.
In the case of the devices he received from Osaka, the seller's address was listed as a house in another city in Japan. That house, the researcher says, is used as an address for numerous companies engaged in various businesses, including criminal enterprises.
More interesting, he says, is that he was able to trace the transmission of the stolen seed data to servers in Hong Kong. The eSIM the attackers planted in Ledger devices is designed to work in any country, and the researcher says that if a device owner doesn't initialize their new wallet, the eSIM still retains the location of the last cell tower it connected to, which he was able to extract from the eSIMs in his wallets.
"This allowed me to find [what I think are] some manufacturing hubs for the implant," he says.
He says additional data contained in the compromised device's microcontroller firmware can be used to trace the location of the command and control servers used to receive the stolen seed phrase. He says he was able to trace the transmissions to servers hosted at a data center in Hong Kong that is managed by Alibaba and determined that in June at least 90 implants on infected Ledger devices were sending seed phrases to those servers, though he thinks the true number of devices communicating with the servers is likely much higher than this.
Pivot to Ledger Flex and Stax Devices
Although most of the compromised Ledger devices so far have been Nano X devices, there is evidence that the attackers have begun to pivot to Ledger Flex and Stax devices. Over the weekend someone posted images of their Stax device on X, which also appears to be compromised. It's not clear if this has been independently confirmed by Ledger or researchers. Separate to this, the researcher in Japan says he purchased two Ledger Flex devices and found implants in them as well.
He says that sometime in July or August he was monitoring a number of online sites that were selling Nano X devices when several of them stopped selling Nano X devices and switched to selling Ledger Flex devices.
"My sense is that they simply developed a new implant that is only for Flex," he says.
He says he has spoken with Japanese law enforcement about his findings as well as with technical contacts at Ledger, but the latter has not shared any information with him about its own investigation.
In the meantime, the list of compromised devices is growing. Over the weekend, Karpelès has been posting information from other Ledger device owners who have since found implants in their devices.
Update 12:30pm EST: SatoshiLabs, the Czech company that makes the Trezor wallets that compete with Ledger products, just announced that in light of implants found in Ledger devices sold by authorized sellers, SatoshiLabs is dramatically reducing its own list of approved sellers. Danny Sanders chief commercial officer for Trezor, wrote on X that the move is a "preventive step" and "there is not a single piece of evidence that Trezor devices have been compromised." In a letter Trezor sent to sellers who will be losing their authorization, Trezor wrote that they continue to sell devices they already have in stock but they will receive no new inventory, and as of January 1, 2027 Trezor will remove them from its list of authorized sellers.
results.summary:
Sophisticated hardware implants discovered in Ledger crypto wallets sold by authorized retailers have enabled a coordinated heist, resulting in the theft of approximately $102 million in digital assets.

### Key Points
- Attackers embedded custom-built antennas and LTE modules into Ledger Nano X, Flex, and Stax devices to intercept and transmit user recovery seed phrases.
- Compromised wallets were identified at authorized resellers, including the Malaysian firm CryptoBilis and the European electronics chain MediaMarkt.
- Blockchain research firm Bitquery confirmed that at least 315 accounts were drained of Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Tron during the recent coordinated attack.
- Security researchers, including Joe Grand and Mark Karpelès, identified multiple generations of increasingly sophisticated, mass-produced hardware implants.
- Data extracted from the implants suggests the stolen seed phrases were transmitted to command-and-control servers hosted in Hong Kong.
- Competitor SatoshiLabs has begun reducing its list of authorized Trezor resellers as a preventive measure against similar supply-chain vulnerabilities.

### Why it Matters
This breach highlights a critical failure in the physical supply chain for hardware security devices, undermining the trust users place in authorized retail channels. The incident forces a reevaluation of security protocols for crypto storage and may lead to stricter distribution controls across the entire hardware wallet industry.

results.title: These Students Thought They Were Making an Investment in Their Future. They Spent Everything They Had. Then the Worst Happened.
results.author: Sarah Butrymowicz
results.content:
This story about cybersecurity training was produced by the Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, independent news organization focused on inequality and innovation in education. Sign up for the Hechinger newsletter.
Looking back, there were a lot of warning signs.
Christopher Collins fielded several calls a day from recruiters with IronCircle, a cybersecurity boot camp provider, urging him to enroll in its online courses. Once he did, they often didn’t function properly, and the help desk was slow to fix issues, he said. He recalled seeing posts on the program’s message boards from graduates saying they couldn’t find work.
But Collins had agreed to a roughly $5,500 payment plan that he would be on the hook for even if he dropped the class. The program was offered through the University of Central Florida, which he felt gave it legitimacy. And returning to his old truck-driving job wasn’t an option because of an injury. He decided to stick it out.
Until the day in June when he couldn’t log in. In emails to Collins, IronCircle first said that a technical issue was to blame, then that fixing the program “remains our top priority.”
By that point, IronCircle was eight days into a liquidation process.
To its critics, including many former students who feel misled by the company, the sudden closure of IronCircle may seem a fitting culmination to its eight years of operation. The company, which had gone through two name changes in that time, regularly charged students as much as $18,900 for classes and then failed to help them get cybersecurity jobs, according to a Hechinger Report investigation that included interviews with more than 35 former students and employees, as well as a review of university records.
Students were sold on the hopes of finding a lucrative job—reviewing security alerts, responding to breaches, testing company systems—at a time of economic uncertainty and rapidly rising costs. In the end, though, they reported the company often gave improbable, deceptive, or false information about job prospects and oversold its own support services.
Still, more than 20 universities, including prestigious public institutions, partnered with IronCircle, offering a de facto seal of approval. The universities earned money—millions of dollars, in some cases—off the arrangement. But IronCircle remained free to operate without following many of the federal rules and regulations designed to protect students.
“When you’re signing up for education offered by an established, reputable university, you’re typically not trying to enroll in a for-profit boot camp dressed up in wrapping paper,” said Aaron Ament, president of the legal advocacy group Student Defense. “Schools that are putting their name on the program have an obligation to oversee it.”
IronCircle officials did not respond to a dozen requests for comment made via email, LinkedIn direct message, and phone in the weeks leading up to the liquidation. QuickStart, the online boot camp provider that announced its acquisition of IronCircle in February, said via email the closure happened outside its control because it had only “acquired certain assets” from IronCircle’s former owner, and said it would let some students transfer into QuickStart courses.
The University of Central Florida did not respond to questions from the Hechinger Report about the abrupt announcement that IronCircle was shutting down. But school officials told Collins in an email that they had been “blindsided” and were working to gather student information to communicate future updates. Other university partners also said they had been caught unaware.
But IronCircle programs had operated with minimal oversight for years. At least one school never collected any program completion or job placement data from IronCircle, according to public record request responses. Others did, and continued the partnership despite incomplete or dismal numbers or despite student complaints.
IronCircle existed in a gray space in the higher education landscape, one populated with several cyber, data science, and coding boot camps that purport to offer people a path into an industry that can be impossible to break into without training. Although it offered programs through accredited universities, it was not accredited itself. Outside officials did not monitor the company’s finances. Its enrollment, completion, and earnings data were not publicly available. And students who needed help paying for the program had to take on private loans, often at much higher interest rates than federal ones and without protections against sudden closures.
The federal government has been slow to regulate these types of companies that partner with accredited universities. In the waning days of the Biden administration, the Department of Education introduced guidance instructing any third-party university partners not to misrepresent themselves as being part of a college and requiring that they follow the same regulations as universities themselves, including when it came to “providing false, misleading or inaccurate information” about “the employability of its graduates.” Department spokesperson Ellen Keast said the guidance remains in effect under the Trump administration, but some experts question how closely anyone is overseeing such companies.
“The Education Department is absolutely not paying attention to this right now,” said Jeremy Bauer-Wolf, investigations manager with the higher education program at New America, a liberal policy group. “It was a struggle to get the Biden administration to do much about it.”
When an admissions representative from HackerUSA, an earlier IronCircle name, phoned Marni Vilardi in May 2021 about a 10-month virtual cybersecurity boot camp run through the University of Michigan, it sounded perfect. (The boot camp would undergo a first name change a few months later, becoming ThriveDX, before changing once more to IronCircle in 2025.)
When the pandemic struck, Vilardi had lost her bartending job. She was serving as a primary caregiver for her ailing mother, while looking for work.
She recalls the company representative telling her that she could expect to make a salary of up to $95,000 right after finishing the program. “Just think,” she remembers the representative saying, “you’re going to be able to hire a private nurse for your mom.” She signed up.
So did Shane Mack. Recruiters with ThriveDX, another earlier name of the company, persuaded him that he could soon make six figures, he said, promoting the program so convincingly that he quit his job as a precision machinist and cashed out his 401(k) plan to cover expenses while enrolled in the University at Buffalo’s program. His ThriveDX classmate RoniKa Griggs recalled being told by a recruiter that 90 percent of the company’s students found jobs, including some before they finished the course. On signing up through the University of Central Florida in 2025, David Young said, he was promised direct connections to people in the cybersecurity field to help find work.
None of it came to pass.
There was good reason for the students to view cybersecurity as a smart career path. The industry was growing, and companies paid well for the positions in an effort to stay a step ahead of hackers.
But the market for cybersecurity workers was becoming flooded. Today, supply for entry-level workers in the industry far outstrips demand. Beginning jobs often require previous work in information technology, often in lower-paying positions, experts say—experience many of IronCircle’s students did not have.
“Entry-level cybersecurity is almost an oxymoron,” said Ira Winkler, a cybersecurity professional and adjunct professor at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County. “Everyone says, ‘There’s a shortage, we should train people.’ There’s a shortage for experienced people who know very specific skill sets.”
IronCircle did not tell prospective students this, according to former students and employees. Instead, they said, under pressure to complete a certain number of monthly sales, many representatives painted a rosy picture of job prospects.
“They want to make the student feel like they’re getting everything on a platter,” said one former IronCircle employee who worked as a learner success manager and career coach. (She was granted anonymity to protect her professional reputation. ) “I just think there was a lot of predatory behavior going on trying to make the sale.”
Many universities contacted for this article did not directly answer questions about allegations made by IronCircle students. The University at Buffalo did not respond to repeated requests for comment. The University of Michigan said it had stopped its partnership with IronCircle due to decreasing interest in the program, while a University of Central Florida spokesperson pointed out that students sign an agreement upon enrolling acknowledging that career services are optional and that the boot camp, in the spokesperson’s words, “does not guarantee job placement upon completion.”
It wasn’t only the recruiters’ assurances that prompted students to sign up for IronCircle’s program. It mattered that respected universities put their names on it.
One of those students was Bret Morris, who took classes with an IronCircle predecessor through the University of Central Florida. He assumed the program had been thoroughly reviewed and was carefully monitored. When he first expressed interest in the classes, “I thought I was actually contacting UCF,” said Morris. “I thought UCF was part of the program.”
IronCircle played up its university connections. Advertisements were emblazoned with university logos and colors. Admissions representatives stressed the partnerships in phone calls, according to former students and employees. Some instructors used university backgrounds images while teaching their courses.
Participating colleges were responsible for signing off on coursework and instructors, according to contracts obtained through a public records request, but IronCircle handled marketing and curriculum development, hired the teachers, and taught all the classes.
Universities each received a percentage of tuition revenue. The University of Nevada, Las Vegas, for instance, earned about $1.8 million through its IronCircle partnership in the 2023–24 school year, records show. From March 2024 to March 2025, IronCircle owed the University of Central Florida nearly $1.2 million, according to a past-due agreement with the school.
“It’s almost like renting out a brand,” said Eileen Connor, president and director of the Project on Predatory Student Lending, a legal group. “It’s really creating consumer confusion. If you didn’t have these university partnerships, I don’t think as many people would be ensnared in this scam.”
Raymond Osorno, a disabled military veteran, enrolled through San Diego State University, assuming the university would only offer a high-caliber program. But he grew skeptical that the course, which he described as “a mile wide and an inch deep,” would help him find a job.
“The school is nothing like it says,” he said. “It’s like having a sticker saying, ‘I did a cyber course.’ ”
He reached out to IronCircle with a litany of questions, including asking them for job placement statistics for the program. The response he received: “We do not track this data.”
San Diego State responded to a records request by the Hechinger Report by saying it did not have responsive documents. A university spokesperson did not answer questions about student outcomes but said that, for all partnerships, the school “sets expectations that programs deliver high-quality instruction, transparent communication to prospective students, and meaningful career development resources.”
In response to records requests, two universities provided reports from IronCircle that contained some job placement data but not enough information to calculate an overall rate. Three universities had complete records. At those, only 35 percent of program graduates were recorded as finding employment within six months.
IronCircle only considered people as having “opted in” to its career services once they had completed a specific set of tasks, public records show. About 55 percent of its students at the three universities met those criteria, and of those, less than two-thirds reported finding a job, according to the data provided by the company.
At the University of Central Florida, IronCircle started tracking the job placement rate of nearly all program finishers beginning in November 2024. Of 325 students, only 26 were recorded as finding a job within six months of completing the program.
When Morris enrolled though UCF, he’d been a stay-at-home dad for 15 years, but recruiters had assured him he would still easily find a job. Career services would work with him one-on-one to help craft a résumé, he recalls being told.
Instead, he said, he was given a generic template. When he raised the issue, he said, his learning success manager suggested he get a job at Best Buy for more work experience.
All of the program completers interviewed for this article reported significant shortcomings with IronCircle’s academic support and career services. They said they had difficulty getting anyone to respond to their questions, and the career guidance they did receive was often unhelpful, mostly involving formatting résumés and LinkedIn profiles.
The former student success adviser and career coach interviewed for this article said she had a caseload of almost 700 students at one point. “It was always a fight for getting on my calendar,” she said.
Kat Kuhlman, who completed IronCircle’s course this February through the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, said she thought she’d find a position through what she called the company’s “exclusive job board.” She discovered it simply aggregated postings from other sources, including Indeed. Many were in information technology, not cybersecurity, or advertised far less money than admissions representatives had told her to expect. One was for a food safety and quality assurance technician and paid a maximum annual salary of $41,600.
Kuhlman ended up working at Jersey Mike’s Subs after finishing her program. “I needed a job,” she said, “because $18,000 for a year of schooling didn’t get me a job.”
UNLV spokesperson Francis McCabe said in an email that hundreds of students had participated in the boot camp through the school since 2021. “There were students who achieved their academic and workforce goals through the program, and unfortunately some who did not,” he wrote. “UNLV has been committed to working with any student who has concerns with the program.”
On June 9, as it did every month, a tuition payment of more than $1,200 hit Rick Stauffacher’s credit card. He was 10 months—and more than $13,600—into his IronCircle boot camp offered through the University of Wisconsin–Madison.
Two days later, he received an email telling him that the program was shut down. (In response to questions, Madison spokesperson Greg Bump said only that the university was 
“winding down its partnership.”)
Stauffacher and other students began scrambling, trying to figure out if they could get their money back. But the options were limited.
Students will be at the bottom of the list to recoup money from liquidation proceedings, experts say. The main private loan lender, Sallie Mae, has no obligation to forgive loans. Students can push universities for a refund, but a sampling of enrollment agreements reviewed by Hechinger say that each agreement is between the student and the company, making the university’s role unclear.
Based on the terms of its acquisition of IronCircle’s assets, QuickStart said, it is not liable financially.
Stauffacher has received regular messages from his payment management company saying his account is delinquent. When he called the company, he said, he was told he would continue to be charged, even though he does not plan to transfer to a QuickStart program. His credit card company initially rejected his application for a refund, he said, but he eventually got $8,000 back.
Stauffacher never heard from UW–Madison, although he noted that the program had been taken off the university’s website. He regrets trusting the school to vet IronCircle’s offerings.
At the time, he said, he thought, “They’re not going to put their name on something they think is terrible.”
But, he added, “I guess they didn’t care, because they were making a bunch of money off of it and not having to do any work besides putting it on their website.”
results.summary:
The sudden liquidation of the cybersecurity boot camp provider IronCircle has left hundreds of students with significant debt and few job prospects despite partnerships with prestigious universities.

### Key Points
- IronCircle, formerly known as ThriveDX and HackerUSA, abruptly shut down in June after eight years of operation.
- The company charged students up to $18,900 for courses while failing to provide promised job placement support or accurate career data.
- More than 20 universities partnered with the firm, earning millions in revenue while providing the program with a veneer of institutional legitimacy.
- Internal data from three partner universities showed only 35% of graduates secured employment within six months of completing the program.
- Students remain liable for private loans and tuition payment plans despite the company’s liquidation and the cessation of all coursework.

### Why it Matters
These partnerships allowed a for-profit entity to leverage the reputations of accredited universities to attract students without being subject to the same regulatory oversight as traditional degree programs. The collapse highlights the risks of "brand renting" in higher education, where institutions prioritize revenue over the vetting of third-party vocational training providers.

results.title: LAYER’s Ripple Dining Table Uses a Wavy Plywood Core to Cut Weight
results.author: JC Torres
results.content:
Large dining tables are useful right up until you need to move one, when their reassuring weight becomes somebody else’s lifting problem. LAYER’s Ripple research table explores a lighter construction by giving thin plywood a corrugated profile instead of relying on a thick slab. That said, the project keeps a flat surface for everyday use while putting the waves underneath, mostly hidden from view.
The original table was specified at approximately 8.2 feet long and 39.4 inches wide, weighing about 19.8 pounds. That’s a generous dining surface for something intended to be moved by one person. Bringing it across a room for guests or shifting it away from the wall could become less of a coordinated household event. Its footprint, however, doesn’t shrink along with its weight.
Designer: LAYER
The material comes from a collaboration with Canadian manufacturer Corelam, using pressure lamination to form the repeating curves. LAYER specifies plywood approximately 0.12 inches thick, although that isn’t the overall depth of the assembled tabletop. The distinction matters here: the design gets its structure from a shaped sheet and layered construction, rather than pretending a thin, flat board can do everything alone.
Of course, a wavy dining surface would be a fairly annoying place to balance your coffee. Ripple covers its corrugated structure with a flat plywood sheet, leaving the waves visible below and along the edge. Plates and laptops get the ordinary surface they need, while the underside carries the more unusual geometry. The useful part doesn’t have to look particularly experimental from above.
The legs follow the same preference for shape over bulk. A refined version uses hollow triangular profiles, designed to increase rigidity in two directions. The tabletop’s underside also curves gently across its length and width. Those changes address a fairly obvious concern with lightweight furniture: being easy to pick up is only useful if the table still supports what you put on it.
The red finish keeps Ripple from disappearing into the background, even with such a thin outline. From the side, the top appears almost like a sheet balanced on four narrow supports. Along the short edges, the repeating curves reveal why that impression is misleading. The structure supplies its own ornament, without adding a carved border or a heavier decorative frame.
Using less wood is part of the environmental argument, too. The project’s original documentation claims 70% to 80% less material than a standard timber table, but doesn’t establish a defined comparison for that figure. Less material isn’t automatically a complete environmental assessment, either. Adhesives, finishing, production, and working life still matter, even when the basic idea of doing more with less is appealing.
LAYER presents Ripple as a studio research project, without a current retail price or ordering details. The construction offers an answer for people whose furniture has to move with them, though size remains a constraint. You might no longer need help with the lifting, but you’d still need a clear route through the house before taking that tabletop around a corner.
results.summary:
The design studio LAYER has developed the Ripple research table, a lightweight dining furniture piece that utilizes corrugated plywood to significantly reduce material weight while maintaining structural stability.

### Key Points
- The Ripple table measures approximately 8.2 feet long and 39.4 inches wide while weighing only 19.8 pounds.
- LAYER collaborated with Canadian manufacturer Corelam to create the table using pressure-laminated plywood sheets just 0.12 inches thick.
- The design features a flat top surface for functionality, with a corrugated underside and hollow triangular legs to provide necessary rigidity.
- The project claims to use 70% to 80% less wood than standard timber tables, though it remains a research concept without retail availability.

### Why it Matters
This design demonstrates how structural geometry can replace material mass to create furniture that is easier to transport without sacrificing surface utility. By reducing the weight of large-format pieces, the project addresses the logistical challenges of modern, mobile living environments.

results.title: Android 17 could soon fix your phone's Wi-Fi and mobile data problems for you
results.author: sanujb6@gmail.com (Sanuj Bhatia) , Sanuj Bhatia
results.content:
What you need to know
- Google is developing new Pixel diagnostic tools to help troubleshoot problems with calls, Wi-Fi, and mobile data.
- The new tools appear under Device Health & Support, alongside existing battery, Bluetooth, and touchscreen diagnostics.
- Pixel phones could soon identify connectivity problems and either attempt a fix or guide users through troubleshooting..
One of the issues we regularly run into on Android phones, unfortunately, is related to mobile data, Wi-Fi, and overall connectivity. But it looks like Android 17 could soon be able to diagnose and fix some of these problems for you.
Google has been building out its Pixel troubleshooting and diagnostics tool for a while now. Pixel phones can already check for issues related to battery health, connectivity, Bluetooth, and even touchscreen problems. But now, it looks like Google is expanding these tools to help users fix calling, Wi-Fi, and mobile data issues as well.
As spotted by Android Police, the recently released Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1, alongside the latest Google Play Services beta, introduces new diagnostic tools designed to troubleshoot problems with calls, Wi-Fi, and mobile data. The new options appear under the Device health & support section.
So, if you're having trouble connecting to Wi-Fi, experiencing dropped calls, or your mobile data suddenly stops working, you'll be able to open the relevant diagnostic tool and have your Pixel check what's going wrong behind the scenes.
Depending on the issue, the tool could either attempt to fix the problem automatically or guide you through the necessary steps to get things working again. This could save users from having to manually dig through network settings or reset their connections every time something stops working.
For now, these new tools have only been spotted in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1 with the Google Play Services beta, so they aren't widely available yet. However, considering they're already showing up in testing, there's a chance Google could introduce them with the stable Android 17 QPR3 release early next year.
Given how frequently Pixel owners have complained about connectivity issues over the years, having built-in tools that can actually help diagnose and fix those problems could be a pretty useful addition.

results.title: Microsoft Breaks Patch Tuesday Record Again with 1400+ CVEs
results.author: Phil Muncaster
results.content:
Microsoft broke records yet again on October 13, releasing more security updates for this month’s Patch Tuesday than in the whole of 2025.
The tech giant fixed 1411 CVEs for October, an all-time high that beat the records it set in July and September this year. By contrast, it released just over 1100 updates in 2025.
The surge in volume can be traced to Microsoft’s use of AI to find and fix vulnerabilities in its products.
Back in July it warned customers to expect a deluge of patches, thanks in part to its use of multi-model agentic scanning harness (MDASH) technology.
The increased workload for security teams is already having an impact. Socura research published this week found that a fifth (22%) of UK CISOs have called in sick or booked holiday time to avoid Patch Tuesday.
The October 2026 haul included one actively exploited and two publicly disclosed zero day vulnerabilities.
The former is CVE-2026-96951, a Windows Shell security feature bypass vulnerability which could lead to malware exposure, data compromise, system integrity violations and operational disruption.
It has a CVSS score of 8.8, involves low attack complexity, and requires no authentication or existing privileges to exploit.
“Attackers can distribute specially crafted files through phishing emails, instant messages, or malicious websites, requiring only user interaction to trigger exploitation,” explained Action1 director of vulnerability research, Jack Bicer.
“The vulnerability can serve as an initial entry point in broader attacks by suppressing expected security warnings and allowing potentially malicious content to bypass protective checks.”
Two New Zero Days Identified
Microsoft also applies the “zero day” label to any vulnerabilities that have been publicly disclosed but not yet exploited in the wild.
One such flaw this month is CVE-2026-108398, a .NET framework security feature bypass vulnerability with a CVSS score of 8.8. It allows authenticated, low-privileged attackers to bypass Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) through an untrusted assembly search path, according to Action1 president, Mike Walters.
“This vulnerability is particularly dangerous as a post-compromise attack technique, enabling attackers with existing local access to circumvent security restrictions without user interaction,” he explained.
“Successful exploitation could compromise system integrity, expose sensitive business information, weaken endpoint defenses and disrupt critical operations.”
With no workaround available and Microsoft labelling this one “exploitation more likely,” sysadmins should patch without delay, Walters advised.
The second publicly disclosed zero day this month is CVE-2026-92707, a denial-of-service flaw in MessagePack-CSharp.
Microsoft explained that an "improperly controlled sequential memory allocation in .NET allows an unauthorized attacker to deny service over a network."
Of the 70 critical vulnerabilities posted this month, most (57) are remote code execution (RCE) flaws. Among the most noteworthy is CVE-2026-70242, a Reading Pane RCE bug in Outlook with a CVSS score of 9.8.
“A crafted email triggers a heap-based buffer overflow when Outlook shows it in the Reading Pane. The recipient doesn't open the message or click anything. No authentication, no user interaction,” warned Automox.
“Preview-pane bugs surface every few years, and they draw attention because email is the front door. Addresses are easy to find in breach dumps and on company websites, so targeting costs an attacker almost nothing.”

results.summary:
Microsoft released a record-breaking 1,411 security patches in October 2026, driven by AI-powered vulnerability scanning, including three critical zero-day flaws requiring immediate attention from system administrators.

### Key Points
- Microsoft’s October 2026 Patch Tuesday update addressed 1,411 vulnerabilities, surpassing the total number of patches released throughout the entirety of 2025.
- The surge in security updates is attributed to the company's use of the multi-model agentic scanning harness (MDASH) technology.
- CVE-2026-96951, a Windows Shell vulnerability with a CVSS score of 8.8, is currently being actively exploited in the wild.
- Two additional zero-day vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-108398 and CVE-2026-92707, were publicly disclosed, with the former posing significant risks to system integrity.
- The update includes 70 critical vulnerabilities, notably a 9.8-rated remote code execution flaw in Outlook that triggers via the Reading Pane without user interaction.
- Research from Socura indicates that 22% of UK CISOs have taken leave to manage the mounting pressure of these frequent, high-volume security updates.

### Why it Matters
The record volume of patches highlights a shift in cybersecurity where AI-driven detection significantly accelerates the identification of vulnerabilities, placing immense operational strain on IT and security teams. Organizations must now prioritize rapid deployment strategies to mitigate risks from actively exploited zero-day flaws that could lead to widespread system compromise.

results.title: 'They're stealing from the poor': A major source of SNAP fraud robs recipients of millions
results.author: Juliana Kim
results.content:
'They're stealing from the poor': A major source of SNAP fraud robs recipients of millions
As Jayeleauna Lewis listened to an automated voice system describe the unauthorized charges on her food assistance card, a pit formed in her stomach. She pictured her 3-year-old daughter and their empty fridge back home.
On the 13th of each month, Lewis, a 20-year-old single mom from Indiana, receives $486 from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, also known as SNAP. But in September, just minutes after funds were loaded onto her account, they disappeared.
" I was heartbroken because that's how I feed my daughter," she says.
Lewis is unsure how her benefits were stolen, but cybersecurity experts say she might have been a victim of skimming — when thieves extract card information from payment terminals and drain money from accounts.
In recent years, SNAP has become a fraud magnet for criminals who view both the nation's poorest Americans and the government program's outdated technology as easy to exploit. The U.S. Department of Agriculture Office of Inspector General projected that, over the past two years alone, $233 million may have been lost due to food assistance theft — largely driven by skimming. And in most states, stolen benefits are not replaced.
The Trump administration has vowed to eliminate SNAP fraud, adding that it's preventing the program from serving those who truly need it. But states' efforts to curb skimming are likely to get harder due to federal funding cuts that began earlier this month, according to Kathryn Larin, a director at the Government Accountability Office, a congressional watchdog agency that has been examining SNAP fraud prevention efforts for years.
"It will increase the budgetary pressure and will make it more difficult for states to allocate funds to benefit card theft prevention," she says.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture, which administers SNAP, told NPR there had been "continued inaction" against skimming long before new funding changes were proposed.
"Skimming has been plaguing recipients for years, and States sat idly, allowing benefits to be stolen from those who need them. SNAP administrative funding changes should not make it harder to fight skimming, as it simply holds these complaining lawmakers accountable," according to a statement from the USDA.
'They know they're stealing from the poor'
Lewis says she has never been to the Northeast. But on Sept. 13, between 12:11 a.m. and 12:13 a.m., her benefits were spent across eight stores in New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Meanwhile, her physical food assistance card, also known as an EBT card, remained tucked in her wallet.
Two weeks earlier, Lewis says she had swiped her card at a gas station to buy a Powerade. Swipe-pay is vulnerable to theft because the magnetic stripe behind cards does a poor job of securing personal information, according to Scott Schober, the CEO of Berkeley Varitronics Systems who has invented several skimming detectors.
It typically goes like this: When a cashier is distracted, fraudsters secretly place a skimming device onto a payment terminal. The device captures troves of card information, which thieves later collect in order to clone cards. With stolen food benefits, criminals typically mass-purchase items that are easy to resell, such as baby formula.
"So it's a very quick ecosystem from the point of stealing the card to drain," Schober says. "Sometimes it's within hours. It's that well-orchestrated."
Skimming first emerged over two decades ago. Most banks in the U.S. have since upgraded their debit and credit cards with microchips that make it harder to copy personal information. SNAP, on the other hand, has lagged in making the switch. Organized criminal rings caught on and zeroed in on food stamp recipients — often timing their theft to the start of each month when benefits arrive, according to Michael Peck, an assistant special agent in charge of the Secret Service's Criminal Investigative Division. Peck oversees the agency's skimming investigations.
"These transnational organized crime groups are coming into the U.S. specifically to target our benefits system," he says. "They know they're stealing from the poor."
The 'human cost' of stolen benefits
Anti-hunger advocates say part of what makes food assistance theft striking is the double standard compared to other victims of fraud.
Christopher Branch, a part-time Walmart employee from Illinois, says he has experienced both credit card and food stamp theft before. While his bank refunded him for the money he lost, the food benefits he used to feed himself and his two children were never recovered. During the month without his food assistance, Branch says he had to take on side jobs such as fixing cars to afford groceries.
" I was very upset and disappointed," he says. "I couldn't get no type of help."
Debit and credit holders are reimbursed for unauthorized transactions under the Electronic Funds Transfer Act. In 1996, Congress voted to exclude SNAP recipients from receiving those same protections due to concerns that it would be too costly, according to a 2025 report by the Government Accountability Office (GAO).
The federal government temporarily replaced more than $320 million in stolen benefits for nearly 670,000 households between October 2022 and December 2024 — giving some insight into the scale of this type of fraud.
But now, there's no federal recourse — so when food assistance disappears, SNAP recipients are forced to make difficult choices. Earlier this year, Propel, an app that helps users check their SNAP balance, surveyed individuals who said they were victims of SNAP theft. A majority of respondents said they skipped or ate fewer meals as a result. Nearly half said they borrowed money or went into debt, while more than a third said they struggled to pay their bills or rent.
"That's the real kind of human cost of SNAP benefits being stolen," says Jimmy Chen, the CEO of Propel.
Then, there's shame. After Mary Barclay from Massachusetts saw her food assistance vanish, she recalled her SNAP caseworker faulting her for not taking more security precautions, like locking her EBT card. When Barclay went to the police, she says her story was met with skepticism.
"They made me feel as if I had something to do with it," she says.
'It can't all be arrests'
In early 2025, California became the first state to start issuing chip-enabled EBT cards. It wasn't a silver bullet, but over the next several months, the state reported a consistent and rapid decline in SNAP theft.
So far, fewer than a third of states have upgraded or plan to upgrade their EBT cards, according to the USDA. States are addressing skimming in other ways, but most of them put the burden on SNAP recipients to be hypervigilant — like changing their card's PIN number on a monthly basis or keeping their cards locked until they're ready to make a purchase.
"It can be difficult for some people to do that if you don't have a cellphone, for example, that has the app that allows you to do the locking," says Larin from the GAO.
On the law enforcement side, federal and state authorities are working to find and remove skimming devices. But Secret Service agent Peck says operations alone can't solve this problem.
"The issue we run into is the fact that the groups that conduct this fraud aren't afraid to go right back to a store and install again," he says.
Funding challenges have compounded
The biggest barrier to chip-enabled cards is cost.
In a report published last year, the GAO found that chip-enabled cards are about 10 times more expensive to produce than magnetic strip ones. The initial transition alone can cost states millions of dollars upfront.
The USDA supports chip adoption, but it provides limited funds to help states do so. For instance, last year, the department awarded seven states a combined total of $5 million to address fraud.
Starting this month, states have fewer federal dollars to operate the food assistance program altogether. That's because of President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut federal funding for states' operational costs by half. At the same time, the law requires state SNAP agencies to focus on reducing their payment error rate — which is a measure of overpayments and underpayments to SNAP recipients — or they'll face harsh financial penalties.
Gina Plata-Nino, the SNAP director for the Food Research & Action Center, says these changes will make it harder for states to combat skimming.
" The likelihood of states being able to switch to chip-tap technology without federal support is going to be even more less likely," she says.
At least five states have said they plan to delay issuing chip cards or related investments as a result of the federal funding changes, according to a survey conducted by the American Public Human Services Association and the Urban Institute earlier this year.
Congress considers mandating chip-enabled cards nationwide. Will it happen?
While modernizing SNAP may be costly and slow, the country has done it before. When states switched from paper food stamps to electronic benefits in the early 2000s, it was largely driven by a desire to prevent food stamps from getting lost, stolen or sold. They did so through federal legislation.
In recent years, Congress has introduced legislation to upgrade EBT cards nationwide or replace stolen food benefits. Right now, the Senate version of the Farm Bill, which provides funding for an array of programs, includes a provision to move toward chips. But the House version does not, meaning it's unclear if the measure will make the final cut. Although the program has bipartisan support, Congress is at a major impasse over SNAP — in particular, the hundreds of millions of dollars possibly imposed on states with high payment error rates.
" The conversation about boosting cybersecurity standards is hard to make as long as Republicans refuse to restore the food assistance," says Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR), who has been pushing for more secure EBT cards since the Biden administration. " What I'm committed to doing is getting both of these over the finish line."
Back in Indiana, Lewis' stolen food assistance has had a ripple effect. Her mother, Johna Hammontree, says she typically lives paycheck to paycheck, but has been stretching every dollar to ensure her daughter and granddaughter do not go hungry.
"It's really, really rough for me already," Hammontree says. "But I will take from my rent money, my bill money, my grocery money … Whatever I need to pull from financially to make sure that she's okay."
results.summary:
Rising rates of skimming fraud are draining millions from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, leaving vulnerable recipients without food benefits as states struggle to fund necessary security upgrades.

### Key Points
- The USDA estimates that $233 million in SNAP benefits may have been lost to fraud over the past two years, primarily through skimming devices.
- Criminal rings target outdated magnetic-stripe EBT cards to clone data, often draining accounts immediately after monthly benefits are deposited.
- Unlike debit card users, SNAP recipients generally lack federal protections to recover stolen funds, forcing many to skip meals or accrue debt.
- California has seen a decline in theft after adopting chip-enabled EBT cards, but the technology is 10 times more expensive to produce than magnetic strips.
- Recent federal funding cuts for state administrative costs have led at least five states to delay or cancel plans for security upgrades.

### Why it Matters
The lack of standardized, secure technology in the SNAP program creates a significant disparity in financial protection between low-income families and traditional banking customers. As federal funding for state operations decreases, the burden of preventing sophisticated criminal theft increasingly falls on the recipients themselves, exacerbating food insecurity for millions.

results.title: Hirudo Android Trojan Uses Patched Banking Apps to Bypass Their Built-In Security Checks
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new Android banking trojan called Hirudo that works by replacing legitimate banking apps with purpose-built patched versions designed to bypass security checks from inside the app itself, marking a new escalation in financial fraud.
Dutch mobile security company ThreatFabric said it identified replacements for eight Indonesian banking apps, while credential targeting in the malware spans Indonesia, China, India, Mexico, Morocco and Thailand.
"The operation combines credential theft, device takeover, screen and camera capture, and SMS theft, in combination with a fairly mature backend," Eward Driehuis, vice president of fraud engineering at ThreatFabric, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.
Hirudo facilitates on-device credential theft and live remote control. The malware is delivered by shopping, adult video, and entertainment dropper apps that carry the trojan as a separate installation package, which is then served as an in-app update.
Some of the dropper apps are listed below -
- Shopora (com.agbbh.kjdrttt)
- 1V1 X (com.onev.vip)
- KoiShort (com.koishort.app)
- ZoyaTV (com.zoyatv.app)
"The lure is functional, loading real content in a WebView, a storefront, a video catalogue or short dramas, so the experience looks legitimate," ThreatFabric explained. "Behind that content the dropper runs a fixed startup routine: it collects promotion-tracking data, fetches its campaign configuration, and checks whether the payload, the Hirudo RAT, is already installed with its accessibility service and notification access enabled."
If it's not present, it displays a fake in-app update prompt to trigger the installation of the malware. It's worth emphasizing that Hirudo is installed as a second app and must be granted its own permissions before it can carry out the malicious activities.
As observed in the case of StreamRat, the malware implements an anti-detection technique based on blocking Internet access by configuring a deliberately non-functional VPN connection prior to the payload installation. This is seen as an attempt to prevent other apps and services, like Google Play Protect, from carrying out cloud-based checks of the payload.
"However, Play Protect also provides offline detection for known potentially harmful applications, meaning that the mechanism does not completely disable its protection," ThreatFabric noted last month. "We therefore assess that the technique is more likely intended to reduce the effectiveness of online reputation and code-analysis mechanisms rather than bypass Play Protect entirely."
Depending on the nature of the lure app used, the dropper is also designed to serve bogus screens to capture payment PINs, serve fake screens requesting login credentials for banks and wallet apps, display fake lock screen pattern and PIN overlays, and facilitate total remote control of the device.
While all this behavior is par for the course when it comes to Android banking trojans, it's their attempts to replace the target banking app with a tampered copy that stand out. Specifically, the purpose-built replacements embed a hooking engine to blind signature, accessibility, screen-capture, and Play Integrity checks from within the app. The replacement targets eight Indonesian apps.
"For these, the RAT detects the installed banking app through accessibility, checks its signing certificate against a stored reference, [and] then shows a fake 'update' prompt," ThreatFabric explained. "It opens Android's uninstaller for the genuine app without waiting for the user to tap, and downloads the bank-specific replacement in parallel."
While the need for having to remove the app before installing its near-identical malicious copy is a "real constraint," the mechanism offers the ability to bypass the banking app's own security checks by returning responses fed by the attacker beforehand.
This involves returning the genuine app signing certificate, returning an empty list when querying for enabled accessibility services, and stripping the FLAG_SECURE flag so that the app's screens can be viewed and recorded remotely.
"Key-attestation certificates are re-signed with a bundled keybox, and Play Integrity requests are relayed over plain HTTP to an operator-controlled server, which returns a verdict for the app to accept," the mobile security company said.
"Two details are worth underlining for defenders. First, the attestation keybox the engine ships is not the operators' own: it is a publicly leaked keybox. Second, because the Integrity request is relayed rather than genuinely produced, a valid Integrity response alone is not evidence of an untampered app."
Evidence indicates that the malware is distributed via fake web pages masquerading as Google Play Store landing pages for shopping, short drama, and football apps. Unsuspecting users are assessed to be directed to these websites through ads on Meta-owned social media platforms.
The entire operation rests on a backend that combines device control with the ability to manage different campaigns and stolen data, including device records, lock-screen history, and financial profiles containing monthly income and risk-score fields.
"Hirudo marks a deliberate escalation in how Android bankers approach hardened applications," ThreatFabric said. "By moving its tampering inside the target app, the operation shifts the contest from the device to the application's own integrity checks, and from a bespoke patch to a reusable engine that can be retargeted at other apps and regions."
"Once an app can be replaced, its locally produced signals, signature, accessibility list, and integrity verdict, must be treated as attacker-influenced and verified server-side," ThreatFabric said.
Last month, the findings came a little over a month after the cybersecurity firm revealed StreamRat's targeting of Spanish-speaking users via Meta and TikTok advertisements impersonating a free TV streaming service named Streamtv Esp to enable control over compromised Android devices.
"StreamRat abuses accessibility services and MediaProjection to provide operators with near-complete control over infected devices, combining VNC and hidden-screen control, UI-tree collection, keylogging, credential-stealing overlays, internet and screen-blocking capabilities," ThreatFabric said.
results.summary:
Cybersecurity researchers at ThreatFabric have identified a new Android banking trojan called Hirudo that replaces legitimate banking applications with tampered versions to bypass critical security and integrity checks.

### Key Points
- Hirudo targets banking apps in Indonesia, China, India, Mexico, Morocco, and Thailand by replacing them with malicious, patched copies.
- The malware is distributed through dropper apps disguised as shopping, entertainment, or adult video platforms, often promoted via social media ads.
- Once installed, the trojan uses a hooking engine to manipulate app signatures, accessibility services, and Play Integrity verdicts to evade detection.
- Attackers gain full remote control of infected devices, allowing them to steal credentials, capture screens, and intercept SMS messages.
- The malware employs a non-functional VPN connection during installation to hinder cloud-based security checks by services like Google Play Protect.

### Why it Matters
This development represents a significant escalation in mobile fraud by shifting the focus from device-level attacks to compromising the integrity of individual banking applications. Financial institutions must now treat locally produced security signals from their apps as potentially untrustworthy and implement more robust server-side verification to protect users.

results.title: How do Iranians move money abroad to avoid US sanctions?
results.author: Tohid Asadi
results.content:
Tehran, Iran – Decades of international sanctions have severely restricted Iran’s access to the global financial system, making cross-border payments difficult for individuals and businesses alike. The sanctions have only increased with the current US-Israeli war on Iran.
Unable to rely on conventional banking for international transactions, many Iranians have turned to alternative channels to pay for goods and services abroad.
And while each workaround channel offers a way to navigate some of the restrictions, it comes with its own costs and risks, often falling short of the security, reliability and efficiency of a functioning international banking system.
One alternative financial channel is relying on networks of currency exchangers that operate across borders, an informal system that matches those who need local currency in Iran with those who need foreign currency abroad. By balancing these opposing needs, transactions can be settled without money necessarily moving directly between Iranian and foreign bank accounts.
There are other similar methods.
Intermediary firms offer services comparable to currency exchange traders. Typically, a customer pays the intermediary in local currency in Iran, while the firm or an overseas partner arranges payment to the foreign supplier in a convertible currency, using funds held abroad.
Using currency traders or intermediary firms can help bridge gaps in international banking access, but both often involve additional fees, exchange-rate costs, delays and greater complexity.
Other Iranians don’t deal with companies, but resort to private arrangements with individuals, including people they do not know personally, to transfer money across borders. Those deals may offer a practical solution when formal channels are unavailable, but they rely heavily on trust rather than enforceable guarantees.
“The transaction involves strangers having to trust one another to conduct a deal without any legal documentation or proof,” said Reza, an Iranian IT manager in Germany, who did not wish to give his full name. “It relies entirely on trust, and either party can back out at any time, leaving the others out of pocket.”
The methods used – whether through companies or individuals – are informal and not the most secure. “We have to use informal exchange and remittance systems for international trade, which carries risks such as lost funds, fraud and high transfer costs,” explained Ashkan Bahrami, an Iranian trade expert.
These networks are also vulnerable to geopolitical shocks. Some operating through Gulf countries have been disrupted by the war, adding another layer of uncertainty for businesses and individuals dependent on them.
The crypto route
Cryptocurrency has offered another route, enabling users to transfer wealth without relying on conventional banks. But even these digital assets have not provided a fully reliable escape from sanctions. Earlier this year, the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned several major Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges, including Nobitex, Wallex, Bitpin and Ramzinex.
Alireza Yaghoubi, chairman of Iran’s FinTech Association board, warned that crypto transactions are traceable, “and very bad things can happen, such as the sanctions imposed on multiple Iranian wallets, whether they belonged to individuals, the Central Bank, or other entities”.
The possibility of sanctions, combined with periodic internet disruptions, makes cryptocurrency an uncertain option.
Import delays
For businesses importing physical goods, the challenges extend beyond payment itself. War-related disruptions and restrictions, particularly after the US naval blockade on Iran, have complicated transportation, lengthened delivery times, and increased uncertainty over when shipments will arrive.
Arghavan Ghazanfari, CEO of Aron Trading Group, described the scale of the disruption facing importers using the port of Shanghai in China, a major gateway for goods shipped to Iran.
“Transit time used to be 26 days. But when it stretches nowadays to 102 or even 120 days, customers are bound to reconsider importing,” Ghazanfari said. “Unfortunately, the main problem now is that our supply routes are gradually being cut off.”
And even when Iranians find a way to make payments abroad – and are willing to accept the delays in receiving their goods – another problem remains: whether they can afford what they are trying to buy.
The Iranian rial’s sustained depreciation has sharply eroded purchasing power. Against the US dollar, Iran’s currency has lost more than 10 percent of its value over the past month, more than 55 percent over the past year and almost 90 percent over the past five years.
And there is little certainty that the pressure will ease anytime soon.
With the prospect of another escalation in the conflict looming over Iran and uncertainty clouding the country’s economic outlook, the question for many Iranians is not simply how to move money across borders. It is how long they can keep navigating an increasingly restrictive financial system, and what it will cost them to do so.
results.summary:
Decades of international sanctions and ongoing geopolitical conflict have forced Iranians to rely on risky, informal financial channels and cryptocurrency to conduct essential cross-border trade and payments.

### Key Points
- Informal currency exchange networks and intermediary firms are being used to bypass restricted access to the global banking system.
- The US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control has sanctioned major Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges, including Nobitex, Wallex, Bitpin, and Ramzinex.
- Supply chain disruptions have increased transit times for imports from ports like Shanghai from 26 days to over 100 days.
- The Iranian rial has lost approximately 90 percent of its value against the US dollar over the past five years, severely eroding purchasing power.
- Geopolitical instability and naval blockades continue to threaten the viability of remaining trade routes and financial workarounds.

### Why it Matters
These financial constraints create significant operational risks for businesses and individuals, including potential fraud, high transaction costs, and total loss of funds. As traditional and digital pathways become increasingly restricted, the long-term sustainability of Iran's import-dependent economy faces growing uncertainty.
