results.title: Ubisoft Is Closing Down Yet Another Studio, Possibly Ending A 25-Year Fan-Favorite Franchise
results.author: John Walker
results.content:
In a statement reported by GI.biz, Ubisoft has announced its “proposal” to close Finnish studio Ubisoft RedLynx, the longtime creators of the fantastic Trials series of motorbike stunt games. This is the latest move in the flailing publisher’s grim 2026, a part of the ongoing “restructuring” of the worldwide network of development teams into so-called creative houses. The latest job losses will also hit Ubisoft Singapore, the team responsible for 2024’s “quadruple A” $200 million-loss disaster Skull and Bones, with 70 staff losing their roles.
For Ubisoft, closing RedLynx isn’t as simple as shuttering some of the other studios it’s killed off over the last year. Finland has specific laws called “change negotiations” or “co-operation negotiations,” which make it a legal requirement for employers to consult with employees before layoffs and large company changes. Clearly closing the 25-year-old studio, acquired by Ubisoft in 2011, would very much fall under those categories, and the law specifically requires such actions to be “anticipatory,” meaning an employer must enter the negotiations before it’s made a decision over the result, hence Ubisoft’s wording saying that this closure is simply a “proposal” at this stage.
RedLynx was already hit hard in 2025 when Ubisoft laid off more than half its workforce, and announced the remaining team would be focused solely on making mobile games.
According to VGC, Ubisoft’s motivation to close down RedLynx and terminate its 52 staff is that “it’s not currently working on a new project, and because “resizing alone wouldn’t keep it sustainable.” In the seven years since the last Trials release, RedLynx aided Massive on the porting of The Division 2 to Google’s doomed Stadia streaming service for 2020, were responsible for the hugely successful porting of Star Wars Outlaws to the Switch 2, and in 2023 released a very short-lived free-to-play mobile match-3 game called Gwen’s Getaway that was taken down after a year, before it ever reached a finished version.
It’s vanishingly unlikely that RedLynx really wasn’t working on anything, not least because Ubisoft previously claimed a year ago that there were two unannounced projects in development, and because what else have the 52 staff been doing? (I’ve been told by someone with direct knowledge on the matter that the team was indeed still working on both projects until very recently.) It also seems hard to believe that the studio wouldn’t be working on a new mobile version of Trials, since the 2D obstacle course format is ideal for touchscreens, and now the tech has caught up enough to prevent a repeat of 2014’s disappointing iOS and Android release Trials Frontier.
It also raises the question of where this leaves Trials. Seven years without a new game has been sad enough, but does the (planned) closure of RedLynx mean the franchise is dead for good? We’ve reached out to Ubisoft to ask for more details.
All at sea
Meanwhile Ubisoft Singapore is being “downsized.” GI.biz reports Ubisoft’s statement as announcing, “At Ubisoft Singapore, 70 positions have been impacted to align the studio with upcoming production needs.” The Singapore studio was originally created to be one of Ubisoft’s international support teams, a group that would work on its colossal AAA games being led by other studios, but eventually took on the Sisyphean task of creating Skull and Bones, an 11-year toil of elaborating Assassin’s Creed‘s naval battles into a full game, that never came together and released to negative reviews and terrible sales.
Since then, the studio took the lead on the far more successful Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced. Sadly, despite selling more than 3.5 million copies in its first two weeks, it hasn’t proven enough to stave off this “downsizing.”
All of this piecemeal “restructuring,” being dragged out so cruelly for so long, certainly isn’t making any difference when it comes to investors’ faith in Ubisoft. Things started to go very wrong in 2021 when the company’s €84 share price began to inexorably tumble, crashing to €3.84 in March 2026, and bumbling along at around €5 since. That represents a 95-percent collapse since its 2018 peak at €100 per share, and it’s showing no signs of recovery.
Updated: 10/15/2026, 3:50 a.m. ET: Added the information that RedLynx was indeed still working on two unannounced projects until very recently.
results.summary:
Ubisoft has proposed the closure of its Finnish studio RedLynx and announced staff reductions at Ubisoft Singapore as part of an ongoing corporate restructuring effort throughout 2026.

### Key Points
- Ubisoft initiated a proposal to close RedLynx, a studio acquired in 2011 that is best known for the Trials motorbike stunt game series.
- The potential closure of RedLynx would impact 52 employees and is currently subject to mandatory Finnish "co-operation negotiations."
- Ubisoft Singapore is downsizing its workforce by 70 positions to align the studio with current production requirements.
- Ubisoft Singapore previously led the development of Skull and Bones, a title that reportedly resulted in a $200 million loss for the publisher.
- Ubisoft’s stock price has declined by approximately 95 percent since its 2018 peak, currently trading near €5 per share as of March 2026.

### Why it Matters
These layoffs reflect Ubisoft's broader struggle to stabilize its finances and operations amid a significant multi-year decline in market valuation. The potential loss of RedLynx raises questions about the future of the Trials franchise and highlights the publisher's aggressive efforts to cut costs across its global development network.

results.title: Attackers chained three Ivanti zero-days to gain root on fully patched VPN appliances
results.author: Zeljka Zorz
results.content:
Attackers chained three Ivanti zero-days to gain root on fully patched VPN appliances
A threat actor has been using an exploit chain combining three vulnerabilities in Ivanti’s Connect Secure (ICS) appliances to breach organizations, collect credentials, exfiltrate configuration data, and perform network reconnaissance.
“In the first week of October 2026, Volexity discovered an unknown threat actor, UTA0576, abusing a zero-day exploit chain to compromise a fully patched (at the time, version 22.8R2.4) Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) VPN appliance,” Volexity researchers shared on Tuesday.
Ivanti says that exploitation affected a limited number of customers at the time of disclosure and that it is working to help those organizations.
How the exploit chain works
According to Volexity, the exploitation chain consists of an authentication bypass (in welcome.cgi), a file write vulnerability (in wu.cgi), and a privilege escalation vulnerability “in how the ICS dsinvoked broker trusts DSCache configuration data, which enables an attacker to execute commands as root.”
This allowed the threat actor to:
- Gain unrestricted access to targeted devices
- Extract credentials stored in it
- Exfiltrate some Active Directory metadata
- Collect local admin passwords and BitLocker recovery keys
- Exfiltrate configuration data
- Capture LDAP traffic from the compromised appliance
- Modify the logs to remove evidence of malicious activity, remove temporary execution artifacts, and perform other cleanup activities.
“Volexity assesses with low confidence that UTA0576 has criminal, rather than espionage, motivations based on the target of this activity,” the company’s researchers said.
“Because the operation was detected and disrupted, the threat actor’s ultimate objectives could not be determined. However, Volexity assesses with high confidence that UTA0576’s actions signaled preparation for lateral movement and a broader compromise of the victim network.”
According to Defused Cyber, the earliest confirmed instance of this attack activity occurred on October 1.
Patches, mitigations, and detection
Ivanti has released a patch for the authentication bypass and RCE vulnerability (CVE-2026-104935), and is working on a fix for the privilege escalation portion of the exploit chain.
“Ivanti initially discovered a portion of this vulnerability as part of our product security program and patched it in the July release 25.1.3.0. We had been working to backport the fix to the remaining supported versions when exploitation occurred,” the company stated.
Ivanti advised customers to upgrade to a fixed release, check for indicators of compromise shared by Volexity, and run ICS’s Integrity Checker Tool regularly, which identify unexpected file modifications on disk.
In this particular case, however, the Integrity Checker Tool may not be of help. “Because this exploit chain patches library code in memory only and restores configuration store data, the tool does not detect any modifications. As such, forensic investigation is required to identify evidence of exploitation,” Volexity noted.
That advice was echoed by CISA, which added CVE-2026-104935 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and ordered US federal civilian agencies to address it and perform forensic triage by October 16, 2026.
Organizations that find evidence of compromise should follow the recovery steps outlined by Ivanti.

A threat actor identified as UTA0576 is exploiting a chain of three zero-day vulnerabilities in Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliances to gain root access and compromise internal networks.

### Key Points
- Researchers at Volexity discovered the exploit chain in early October 2026, affecting fully patched Ivanti Connect Secure version 22.8R2.4.

- Compromised appliances allowed attackers to steal credentials, exfiltrate Active Directory metadata, and capture LDAP traffic while modifying logs to hide their activity.
- Ivanti has released a patch for CVE-2026-104935 and is working on additional fixes, while CISA has ordered federal agencies to perform forensic triage by October 16.

Organizations relying on VPN appliances must prioritize forensic monitoring, as these sophisticated attacks can facilitate lateral movement and long-term network compromise.

results.title: If you've sworn off genAI Crazy Taxi and dislike all the twerking in GTA 6, consider Shifu: Traffic Masters, a jolly open world driving game set in 1990s China
results.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
results.content:
I'm not your guy for computerised automobile magic picture shows, or "car videogames" as they are popularly known – for that, we turn fearfully to Mark Warren, whose every word during Gchat meetings is screamed against a backdrop of throbbing motors. Still, once in a blue moon a car game hooks my interest. Take Shifu: Traffic Masters, which we can approximately translate as Driver and/or Midtown Madness (those are explicit inspirations), but set in northern China during the 1990s. It's got a demo on Steam. Cars emit steam, don't they? How poetic of them. Here's a trailer.
In Traffic Masters, you've got a selection of vehicular pursuits to choose from. You can haul cargo with real physics, chase down crims in a cop car, run a taxi service (don't jostle the passenger too much), drive a city bus with a timetable, and participate in full-blown arcade street racing. All the traditional car game foods. You'll be doing this in a city inconsiderately populated by pedestrians and cyclists, in which weather affects the handling. You're free to explore said city between jobs, getting to grips with various low poly "period-correct '80s and '90s workhorses, each with its own weight and personality".
That's "personality" as in the unfathomable feeling that an inanimate object has wiles and foibles, rather than in the latter-day sense of a Muskian chatbot chauffeur. This is set in the previous millennium, remember, when machines were very often genuinely quite fun to be around. Although we did have actual "Traffic Masters", aka traffic congestion notifications with old-timey robot vocals. My dad had one that always seemed to think he was on the M25. On which note, there's no mention of generative AI on the Shifu: Traffic Masters Steam page, but in these Crazy times of publishers having to revise their Steam disclosures following a backlash, we must gaze at everything through narrowed eyes.
It comes in Chinese and English, and is the work of solo dev Boxy.Poly. There's no release date yet.

results.title: NostradamusGPT: The Psychology of Prophecy and How to Break Free from the Prison of Predictive Technologies
results.author: Maria Popova
results.content:
NostradamusGPT: The Psychology of Prophecy and How to Break Free from the Prison of Predictive Technologies
By Maria Popova
This is our paradox: We know that uncertainty is the substrate of the universe, is the crucible of creativity, is the path to truth, and yet we spend our lives searching for certainty. The word auspicious derives from the Latin auspex — one who examines the flight of birds for omens and divinations of the future. Today, our birds are made of bits — wind-up larks of our own making we call algorithms — but they serve the same function: to let us believe that we can divine the future in order to respond to it; to sedate our anxieties of living by selling us the illusion of control over the unknowable.
All power structures are prisons we choose to live inside and all prediction technologies are power structures. Prophets have always been the true governors of empires, first counsels to kings, final ventriloquists of the future.
We can never break free from the uncertainties of living, for we ourselves are bright violations of probability, but we can break free from the prison of prediction in order to be more alive: The great mercy of life is that we can change, we can reroute, we can surprise ourselves — that our future is not the computational sum of our past and our destiny not a deterministic equation but an ongoing process constantly creating itself, the way a memory reconstitutes itself with each retelling. Every algorithm that tries to tell us what we will like or do next based on what we have liked or done previously is stealing our self-respect — the respect for the fundamental capacity for self-surprise that makes life worth living — and selling it back to us at the price of the product.
How to defend this vital aspect of our humanity, of life itself, from the merchants of prediction is what Carissa Véliz explores in Prophecy: Prediction, Power, and the Fight for the Future, from Ancient Oracles to AI (public library) — a book that, in an epoch when it is difficult to say anything original about AI, offers a revelatory look at the prison we have chosen to live inside and a key out.
She writes:
The computer scientists of today play the same role in power and prophecy as the oracles of the ancient world, the astrologers of the Middle Ages, and the social scientists of the nineteenth century, as we will see… Prophets are merchants of prediction… Artificial intelligence is the new Oracle of Delphi. The likes of Elon Musk, Sam Altman, and Eric Schmidt sharing drinks with presidents and prime ministers is reminiscent of Nostradamus advising Catherine de’ Medici, and Rasputin counseling Nicholas II.
[…]
Predictions are often power moves disguised as quests for knowledge. Even when predictions are sincere, they can create currents of political influence that change the world. They become power moves.
She offers a fascinating history of how such technologies of power became possible, became desirable, became the norm — a history that chronicles the shift from the spiritual to the statistical, from faith to blind trust:
With God gradually moving into a background position, the grip of fate loosened. Along with worldviews that could make sense of and contemplate the notion that chance might play an important role in the world, the invention of printing with movable type in the middle of the fifteenth century facilitated the development of abstract numerical thinking, and with it, scientific inquiry and bureaucratic organization.
[…]
Trust in numbers was partly born out of distrust in people.
It was not only the Church’s disapproval that led to a decline in traditional forms of divination; common people were tired of depending on experts to catch a glimpse of the future. Reading animal entrails or the flight of birds is not obvious, and astrology is technical. The opaqueness of these methods facilitated fabrication, errors, and corruption. Divinatory lots such as dice are ways of potentially communicating with the gods in an open way, visible and readable to all. They also invite asking questions about randomness and probability, which might have contributed to probabilistic thinking. But dice were unfit for purpose in the Enlightenment and beyond. Games of chance were associated with gambling and vice, and leaving decisions to pure chance was counter to rationality. Statistics came to the rescue.
After getting a kick start from astronomers, statistics developed mostly thanks to bureaucrats who were responding to challenges in public life. It was a practical endeavor, not a scientific one. Merchants, bankers, farmers, militaries, and tax officials needed to count in standardized ways. Extensive trade needs prices and measures, and therefore extensive quantification. As bureaucracies grew, standardization and public justification were necessary. There was also the question of how to hide power struggles to make them look as rational as possible. Numbers, standards, and statistics make politics and power invisible. That’s convenient to anyone wanting to justify what they do as free from values.
Behind our trust in numbers is a closely related philosophical idea: that values cannot be derived from facts.
Which, of course, they cannot. None of the things we most value — not mountains, not music, not love — can be reduced to a set a facts. Numbers and figures can contour for us what the world is — truly or falsely — but they can never shade in how to live in it, how to share it, how to reshape it into the kind of world we want to live in. Statistical probability will never tell us anything about the reach of possibility. Probability theory pioneer Marc Kac himself recognized that all creative acts — those triumphs of our humanity — spring from “a world with its own passions, elations and despairs, and it is here that… one may even hear the voice of God.”
Véliz counters the cultural myth we have been sold:
The world is not inherently statistical; we made it so by quantifying it, the better to control it.
Statistics invented society. Since the statistical regularities in phenomena like crime and suicide could not be traced to individual actions, these patterns became attributed to “society” itself. Society became a living entity, above and beyond the individuals constituting it. From 1830, these numerical regularities were interpreted as the most compelling evidence of society’s existence. Statistics invented normal people too.
[…]
Probabilistic thinking changed our views of reality (our metaphysics), how we think about what we know (our epistemology), what we count as a good argument and an explanation (our logics), and how we think of the good life (our ethics). It might have even changed the way we think about how we think.
It didn’t just change us, it killed something essential of our nature — the shimmering irregularity that makes each of us who we are, a singular constellation of atoms and story unmatched in all the history and future of the universe. She writes:
The murderers were philosophers, gamblers, mathematicians, sociologists, insurers, and, above all, bureaucrats. The murder weapons were quantification, data collection, and statistical tools like the normal curve… The motive was power, understood broadly: from astronomers wanting to predict the skies for the purposes of navigation and timekeeping, to insurers wanting to make a profit, to bureaucrats vying for authority and wanting to have more control over the population. We killed individuals with names, personalities, and idiosyncrasies. We killed valuing people for who they are, without attaching categories, numbers, or, worse, rankings to them. We killed our confidence in free will, a topic to which we will come back in chapter eight. We killed trust in people and replaced it with trust in numbers. We gained order, but it came at a price. What we lost is rarely subject to quantification. But that it cannot be quantified doesn’t mean that it didn’t exist or matter.
In a passage that calls to mind Ursula K. Le Guin’s eternal insistence that “words are events, they do things, change things,” she adds:
We do things with words, other than describe the world. Predictions are not mere assertions; they are acts in the world, and that is a further reason why they are not facts. Predictions are speech acts: assertions that do something.
[…]
When someone makes a prediction, depending on the context and their methods, as well as their will to power (what they want), they might be doing very different things: expressing their degree of confidence about something, expressing the chances of something happening in the world, expressing what they want the world to look like in the future, trying to manipulate their audience into buying what they sell, or a combination… What they are not doing, however, is uttering a true statement about the world.
[…]
Predictive societies tend toward oppression through surveillance and self-fulfilling prophecies because predictions are speech acts that are closer to commands than to truth claims.
Given our cognitive apparatus is wired for our expectations to shape our reality, the predictions we believe end up shaping our lives:
A prediction about people has reflexive qualities, acting like a magnet that bends reality toward itself. When the force of the magnet is strong enough, the prediction becomes the cause of its becoming true.
[…]
Predictions are commands disguised as descriptions… Predictions change the reality they purport to predict, and sometimes their accuracy is evidence not of knowledge or understanding but of despotism.
Our greatest frontier of resistance is to remember that we can be the makers of our own destiny with our choices, but our choices are driven by our beliefs, which are the easiest thing to manipulate and imprison in a power structure, and therefore the first thing that must break free. Véliz — who delves deeper into these questions in this excellent Where Shall We Meet interview — insists that the key is in our hands if we keep in mind — our gloriously fractal, wildly associative, defiantly illogical mind — a few truths about being human that the prophets of prediction try to obscure:
- What we deem inevitable often never comes to pass, while what we thought impossible awaits around the corner.
- Spaces of indeterminacy are where creativity, humor, and innovation flourish.
- Allowing defiance is the right way to treat human beings, who are ends in themselves, with their own idiosyncratic views and preferences. Every life is worth living, every life a work of art to be created much more than discovered.
- We shape our ideas and our ideas shape us
Reflecting on the tapestry of paradoxes threading through our yearning for control and our vulnerability to exploitation, she asks:
Unpredictability, arising from partial knowledge, social complexity and reflexivity, scientific and technological breakthroughs, flukes, and blindness, is never going away. Given this unsettling fact of life, how should we live?
The best answer I know is this Marie Howe poem.
			—
Published October 13, 2026
—

—

results.title: The biggest GOP lie isn’t about elections — it’s the economy
results.author: Kirk Swearingen
results.content:
Donald Trump lies. Telling untruths is not merely second nature to him; it is of the first order, automatic. He lies as naturally as he breathes.
From his claim to being a great businessman and dealmaker to calling himself not the worst president in U.S. history — which he is, by far — but the best, Trump has spewed a firehose of falsehoods to the public. But he has never reserved his lying only for his political opponents.
He has lied to his MAGA followers about, well, everything — bringing grocery prices down, ending this or that war “on day one,” the value of his cryptocurrency offerings, creating any number of “unbelievable” plans to fix our infrastructure, our healthcare, our economy. All those “beautiful” plans that were never plans but so-called concepts of plans. You know, back-of-the-envelope musings on critical national issues while heading off for another taxpayer-funded golf outing.
Suffice it to say: If you can name it, Trump has lied about it.
Journalists often write of Trump’s Big Lie about how the 2020 election was stolen from him, but that is only one of the big lies Republicans tell, and it is not the one that most adversely affects working Americans.
With Trump’s wild mismanagement of the economy, public sentiment is finally changing. More people now trust Democrats on the economy, and for good reason.
The biggest lie is the one Republicans have told for more than half a century — about how they are better than Democrats at managing the economy. A majority of Americans have believed this for my whole lifetime. But with Trump’s wild mismanagement of the economy, public sentiment is finally changing. More people now trust Democrats on the economy, and for good reason.
The idea of telling a lie so massive that not many people would think that it could be made out of whole cloth comes from Adolf Hitler’s 1925 book “Mein Kampf.” The failed artist and future German führer thought that most people would not believe that someone “could have the impudence to distort the truth so infamously.” This theory was later put to use by Joseph Goebbels, the Third Reich’s propaganda minister, to scapegoat and dehumanize Jewish people, and it led directly to the Holocaust — a horrible truth many Nazi-curious conservatives love to deny.
Trump, a fanboy of ruthless dictators, was determined to stay in office after losing the 2020 election decisively in both the Electoral College and the popular vote to Joe Biden, and he naturally turned to Hitler’s technique. (I say “naturally” because, according to his first wife Ivana, he kept a volume of Hitler’s speeches by his bedside. Also, after Trump’s first term, his former White House chief of staff Gen. John Kelly warned Americans that Trump very much admired Hitler.)
The Republican’s lie on the economy is such a whopper — so “colossal,” as Hitler put it — that it has defined American politics for decades. That’s the ruse of the colossal lie, which is not merely the propagandist’s use of repetition (Trump’s main go-to move) but a sort of verbal legerdemain. People are cunningly led to disbelieve what they see with their own eyes and feel in their own pocketbooks.
As we head into the November midterms, and as candidates begin to emerge in the 2028 presidential race, it’s a good time to refresh our memories of how costly the GOP’s colossal lie about trickle-down economics, which began with President Ronald Reagan, has been for Americans.
Running for the presidency, the former Republican California governor and B-list actor said that giving tax breaks to the wealthy and corporations would “trickle down” benefits to the working people of America. This sounded good in theory, but it was “voodoo economics” in practice, as George H. W. Bush, Reagan’s opponent in the 1980 Republican primaries, noted — until he was chosen as the Californian’s running mate).
In his two terms, Reagan’s tax cuts increased the national debt from $1.1 trillion to $2.7 trillion. But that’s nothing compared to Trump. While occupying the White House, the president has increased the national debt by a staggering $11.6 trillion so far, an increase of more than 25%.
As I’ve written before, Democratic presidents have almost always done better — I should say much better — than Republican presidents in managing the U.S. economy. According to a 2016 academic study by Alan S. Blinder and Mark W. Watson, this was true from the Truman administration through the first Obama term across all major macroeconomic measures: job creation, unemployment, national debt, GDP growth, growth in real wages and controlling inflation.
As Blinder and Watson concluded:
[T]here is a systematic and large gap between the U.S. economy’s performance when a Democrat is president of the United States versus when a Republican is. Democrats do better on almost every criterion.
We can tack on Biden’s term as well, which, amid the global inflation spikes caused by the COVID-19 pandemic shutting down supply chains, recovered far better than any other advanced country. As The Economist put it at the time, the quickly recovering economy under Biden was “the envy of the world.” People may not have felt “the vibe,” but things were on the right track by all standard economic measures.
In addition, in 2021, the Biden administration’s $1.2 trillion Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act was passed with bipartisan support to rebuild or upgrade the nation’s aging transportation, water and broadband systems. The following year, the $280 billion CHIPS and Science Act was enacted and called for microchip manufacturing to be started up in rural areas, mostly Republican-voting districts. Unlike Trump, Biden understood that the president is charged with working on behalf of all Americans, not just those who voted for him.
Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.
Since the Republican President Dwight Eisenhower, about 70% of all jobs have been created during Democratic administrations, and in recent decades, the percentage is more than 90%. Of the 11 recessions the country suffered between 1953 and 2020 — when the pandemic began — 10 began while a Republican was in the White House.
What Blinder and Watson studied was independently updated in 2024 with similar findings of a “striking” positive difference on the U.S. economy when a Democrat is in the White House. One doesn’t need academics or economics experts to tell that Republicans never look out for the interests of the working class, or even the middle class. But for those who still like evidence, a series of charts by Steven Rattner and graphic artist Taylor Maggiacomo tell the story of Trump’s promises on the economy and his results so far.
What these charts cannot show is the long-term economic disaster of lost markets for farmers and U.S. manufacturers caused by Trump’s tariffs and his disparagement of our trading partners, or what it will mean to our economy as countries move to de-Americanize their tech — which they must do to protect themselves from Trump.
Democrats are not only better stewards of the economy, but they also want the wealth created by American workers to be shared more equitably and for the social safety net to be made more robust, so Americans can better weather any financial vicissitudes.
Although he had once headed the Screen Actors Guild, Reagan kicked off the GOP’s modern union-busting zeal, treating union members as badly as he did university kids, our infrastructure of the future, as governor of California. This points to another factor that macroeconomic statistics do not tell us: Democrats are not only better stewards of the economy, but they also want the wealth created by American workers to be shared more equitably and for the social safety net to be made more robust, so Americans can better weather any financial vicissitudes.
Democrats also understand that the economy depends on healthy, educated, informed workers, and that the performance of parents in the workforce increases when they have access to affordable quality childcare.
Do I need to point out that Republicans have little to no desire to help workers and those in need, outside of, say, charitable contributions or church work? Indeed, rather than looking out for the poor or loving the stranger — and growing increasingly annoyed by those darned Biblical verses about a camel passing through the eye of a needle — the wealthy and powerful long ago undertook to remake American Christianity.
As Salon’s Amanda Marcotte recently noted, the right’s perversion of the message of Jesus knows no bounds; to justify their greed and avarice, they are taught that it is inconceivable to be Christian and vote other than Republican, which is yet another colossal lie by the GOP.
Public sentiment about which party does best in managing the economy has finally shifted to Democrats in the face of Trump’s gross mismanagement of the recovering Biden economy. Trump’s tax cuts, tariffs, attacks on education and journalists, his disparagement of historical allies and his war of choice with Iran have undermined nearly every aspect of what has made the United States prosperous.
But it is up to journalists to regularly tell this truth to the public in the face of the colossal Republican lie about the economy that began with Reagan, a man who had the sheer audacity to claim that the budget deficit was affected by restaurant servers not declaring their tips.
Today’s Republicans are even more Dickensian, focused as they are on deporting hard-working immigrants who long to be American citizens and taking healthcare and even food stamps away from struggling American families.
Why are Republicans terrible with the economy? Because they do not believe in government — unless it helps them.

Standard Chartered expands Bitcoin and Ether trading to professional investors in UAE
Standard Chartered expanded its spot crypto trading services to professional investors in the UAE region, with plans to offer access to more market participants.
Standard Chartered has expanded Bitcoin (BTC) and Ether (ETH) trading to wealthy clients in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) who qualify as professional investors.
Eligible investors can trade these assets within their existing Standard Chartered bank accounts, the London-headquartered multinational bank announced Wednesday.
Standard Chartered’s eligibility criteria require individuals to have at least 4 million dirhams (about $1.1 million) in net assets, excluding their main residence, and sufficient investment knowledge and experience or representation by a licensed entity.
Digital assets are “moving into mainstream wealth conversations,” and the bank’s clients are increasingly looking for the “security, trust and confidence that comes from investing through a regulated and trusted institution,” said Samir Subberwal, global head of wealth solutions, retail products, data and analytics at Standard Chartered.
The development comes over a month after Standard Chartered launched UAE crypto trading services for institutional clients in early September.
Standard Chartered is not the only company expanding its digital asset offering in the region. On Monday, cryptocurrency exchange Kraken’s parent company, Payward, received VARA approval to provide crypto services through its local entity. In July, neobank Revolut received in-principle approval from Dubai’s VARA to offer crypto-related services.

results.title: 7 EDC Backpack Brands Worth Your Attention, With One Pick From Each
results.author: Rei Padla
results.content:
Finding a reliable everyday carry backpack isn’t as simple as choosing one with enough room for your laptop. A bag might have plenty of compartments but make frequently used items difficult to reach. Another might look great in photos but feel unnecessarily bulky during a commute. When you’re carrying the same equipment every day, small design problems become difficult to ignore.
The best EDC backpacks balance storage, accessibility, and comfort without making you carry more bag than you need. Some prioritize laptop protection and office essentials, while others are better suited to camera equipment, travel, or smaller accessories. The challenge is finding a backpack that matches how you actually use it.
We’ve selected seven brands with established reputations for practical backpack design, along with one model from each worth considering. These recommendations focus on specifications, features, and everyday usefulness rather than unverified claims about long-term durability or comfort.
1. Aer: City Pack Pro 2 24L
Aer has built its reputation around backpacks designed for commuting and travel, with an emphasis on practical storage and understated styling. The brand is particularly appealing to people who carry electronics and want a bag that doesn’t look out of place in a professional setting.
Price:  $219
Where to Buy: Aer
The Aer City Pack Pro 2 24L features a 1680D CORDURA ballistic nylon exterior, YKK zippers, and a padded compartment designed to accommodate most 16-inch laptops.
Its main advantage is the lay-flat opening, which provides easier access to clothing, headphones, and larger accessories. Two exterior bottle pockets and a luggage pass-through also make it useful for short trips.
At approximately 2.86 pounds empty, it isn’t the lightest option. However, its combination of everyday organization and packing space makes it a sensible choice for someone who wants one backpack for work and occasional overnight travel.
2. Bellroy: Transit Workpack Pro 22L
Bellroy approaches everyday carry with a focus on streamlined designs that work in professional and casual environments. Its backpacks generally avoid excessive exterior straps and bulky compartments, making them appealing to people who prefer a cleaner appearance.
Price:  $249
Where to Buy: Amazon
The Bellroy Transit Workpack Pro 22L is designed for people who regularly move between offices, cafés, and airports. Its 22-liter capacity provides room for daily work essentials without moving into oversized travel-backpack territory.
The Transit range emphasizes accessible storage for electronics and smaller belongings. That approach is useful when you frequently need to retrieve a laptop, charger, or travel document without unpacking everything else.
The main limitation is capacity. Someone who routinely carries gym clothes, bulky equipment, and work accessories together may need something larger. For professionals who travel light and prefer a discreet design, the Transit Workpack Pro is worth considering.
3. EVERGOODS: CIVIC Half Zip 22L
EVERGOODS focuses on practical backpack construction, with designs that combine outdoor-inspired materials and everyday functionality. Its bags are particularly appealing to people who prefer straightforward layouts over complicated internal organization.
The EVERGOODS CIVIC Half Zip 22L uses a traditional half-zip opening, making it familiar to anyone accustomed to conventional daypacks. Its 22-liter capacity is suitable for a laptop, notebook, water bottle, and other daily essentials.
Price:  $215
Where to Buy: Evergoods
The CIVIC Half Zip combines a roomy main compartment with dedicated storage for electronics and smaller essentials. An external suspended laptop pocket, quick-access lid pocket, internal stretch sleeve, and two security pockets provide organization without a camera-style divider system.
The trade-off is access. A half-zip opening makes items near the bottom less convenient to retrieve than a full clamshell design. This backpack is better suited to someone who values a simple layout and doesn’t need to access every item frequently.
4. Peak Design: Everyday Backpack 20L
Peak Design is best known for bags and accessories designed around photography equipment. Its approach to backpack organization is particularly useful for people who need to access cameras, lenses, and electronics throughout the day.
The Peak Design Everyday Backpack 20L features FlexFold dividers, side-access zippers, and a MagLatch top closure. These features allow users to organize equipment while keeping frequently needed items within reach.
Price:  $279.95
Where to Buy: Amazon
The dividers can also accommodate everyday accessories, making the backpack useful beyond photography. However, its structured interior is less convenient for people who regularly carry bulky clothing or oddly shaped objects.
This is the strongest option on our list for photographers and content creators. Its specialized layout makes more sense for equipment that benefits from separated storage than for someone who simply needs a large compartment for daily belongings.
5. TOM BIHN: Synik 22
TOM BIHN has a long history of producing bags designed around practical organization. Its backpacks tend to favor accessible compartments and functional layouts rather than minimalist styling.
The TOM BIHN Synik 22 offers 22 liters of capacity, five exterior pockets, and a full clamshell opening. It also includes a suspended laptop compartment, removable internal frame, and luggage pass-through.
The exterior pockets are particularly useful for separating smaller items such as charging cables, notebooks, and travel documents. Meanwhile, the clamshell opening makes the main compartment easier to pack when carrying clothing or larger accessories.
Price:  $345
Where to Buy: Tom Bihn
Its suspended laptop compartment fits most 13-inch laptops, so buyers carrying larger devices should check TOM BIHN’s compatibility guidance carefully. The Synik 22 is also a premium-priced backpack, making it more appealing to people who specifically want its compartment layout rather than a basic laptop bag.
6. Able Carry: Daily Plus
Able Carry designs backpacks around everyday mobility, with particular attention to weight distribution and keeping the exterior relatively uncluttered. Its approach suits commuters who carry a moderate amount of equipment but don’t want a large travel backpack.
The Able Carry Daily Plus offers 21 liters of capacity, a laptop sleeve designed for most 16-inch devices, and a separate tablet compartment.
Price:  $188
Where to Buy: Able Carry
One of its more distinctive features is the concealed water bottle pocket, which keeps the bottle accessible without adding a conventional exterior holder. Its A-Frame support is designed to keep the pack supported under heavier loads, although comfort will vary depending on the user and how the bag is packed.
The Daily Plus is a good fit for someone who wants dedicated electronics storage and a compact exterior. Buyers should compare the available materials and weights before choosing a configuration.
7. ALPAKA: Elements Backpack Pro
ALPAKA produces bags and accessories aimed at people who carry electronics and smaller everyday essentials. Its backpacks typically use multiple storage sections to keep equipment separated.
The ALPAKA Elements Backpack Pro offers approximately 24 liters of capacity, dedicated laptop storage, and an organization panel for accessories.
Price:  $189
Where to Buy: Amazon
This arrangement works well for someone who carries a laptop, power bank, headphones, charging cables, and other work essentials. Instead of placing everything inside one compartment, smaller items can be kept in designated pockets.
The downside is reduced flexibility for larger objects. A backpack with numerous dividers may be less convenient for carrying bulky equipment than one with a simpler interior. The Elements Backpack Pro is best suited to commuters who prioritize keeping their electronics organized.
Which EDC Backpack Should You Buy?
Choosing between these backpacks comes down to what you carry and how you prefer to access it. The Aer City Pack Pro 2 is a strong all-around option for work and short trips, while Bellroy’s Transit Workpack Pro suits professionals who prefer a streamlined appearance. EVERGOODS offers a simpler daypack layout for people who don’t need extensive compartments.
Photographers should consider the Peak Design Everyday Backpack, while the TOM BIHN Synik 22 is better suited to people who appreciate separate pockets for smaller belongings. Able Carry offers a compact alternative for daily commuting, and ALPAKA is worth considering if your bag regularly carries numerous electronic accessories.
Before ordering, check the laptop compartment dimensions, backpack weight, and opening style. Capacity alone doesn’t tell you how easily a bag will accommodate your equipment, particularly when internal dividers take up space.
A good EDC backpack should make carrying your essentials easier without adding unnecessary bulk or complexity. These seven brands offer different approaches, but the right purchase is the one that fits your equipment, routine, and budget.

results.title: The iPhone Duo Is Solving A Big Comfort Problem With Folding Phones - Here's How
results.author: staff@bgr.com (Joshua Hawkins)
results.content:
The iPhone Duo Is Solving A Big Comfort Problem With Folding Phones - Here's How
There has been a lot of excitement around the iPhone Duo since Apple announced it back in September, 2026. Despite its starting price of $1,999, most people have spent their time focusing on the design and the cool new features exclusive to the iPhone Duo. However, there's one development that you might not think about that heavily when looking at the first device in Apple's foldable line-up, and that's how Apple appears to have solved a long-standing comfort problem for foldables: Heat.
Heat is one of the biggest engineering challenges in electronics, and it's responsible for all manner of issues and tradeoffs. Heat can cause all sorts of performance issues. It also puts more strain on electrical components and cause them to degrade faster overall.
Foldables struggle with this issue even more than a typical smartphone, since the design stacks two sides of the potentially hot screens and components against one another, changing how heat radiates in the process. That includes the iPhone Duo, which doubles in thickness when it's closed. Banafsheh Barabadi, Apple's senior manager of thermal product design, called it one of the most challenging parts of creating the device. So how did Apple overcome this particular problem? Well, in an interview with PC Magazine, he detailed how the company ended up using the Duo's hinge to help.
How the iPhone Duo's hinge helps keep it cool
Like the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, the iPhone Duo relies on a vapor chamber to help pull heat away from its A20 Pro chip. In the case of the iPhone Duo, that thinner vapor chamber sits in the middle of the phone. And because the phone is basically two pieces stuck together with a hinge, Apple had to find some way to spread that heat out so it didn't accumulate in one place. The answer came from a graphite pipe in the design, which carries heat through the hinge to the rest of the phone, allowing it to dissipate along the way.
Apple's thermal and mechanical teams worked together on the part, since it has to keep moving heat while also surviving being repeatedly opened and closed throughout the life of the device. That's a lot to ask of a single part, especially one that you're going to be bending every single time you open your phone.
Apple also says that all of this work helps the iPhone Duo offer up to 35% better sustained performance compared to the iPhone 17 Pro, and the company's engineers have said they expect it to run just fine without overheating. Of course, those are still Apple's own claims, and we haven't seen any independent testing of the iPhone Duo's thermals just yet. So, if you're planning to pick one up, and use it for gaming, you might want to wait until the first reviews arrive before spending $1,999 on Apple's first foldable.
results.summary:
Apple has addressed thermal management in its new $1,999 iPhone Duo foldable by utilizing a specialized graphite pipe within the hinge to dissipate heat from the A20 Pro chip.

### Key Points
- The iPhone Duo features a unique thermal design that routes heat through the device's hinge to prevent accumulation when the phone is closed.
- Apple integrated a thin vapor chamber alongside a flexible graphite pipe to manage temperatures generated by the A20 Pro processor.
- Thermal product design manager Banafsheh Barabadi noted that the hinge mechanism was engineered to maintain heat transfer while enduring repeated folding.
- Apple claims the new cooling system provides up to 35% better sustained performance compared to the previous iPhone 17 Pro model.

### Why it Matters
Effective thermal management is critical for foldable devices, which often struggle with heat dissipation due to their compact, multi-layered construction. If successful, this engineering solution could set a new industry standard for performance stability in high-end foldable smartphones.
